visual.title: One call to holiness, several states of life, and a doctrine/discipline test
visual.description: A branching map of the states of life with a separate decision test attached, so that ordination, celibacy and consecrated life are not confused.
steps: At the top, a single bar labelled UNIVERSAL CALL TO HOLINESS (LG 39–42): all the faithful, no exceptions, no state of life excluded.
Three branches down: MARRIAGE (covenant, CCC 1601); CONSECRATED LIFE (public profession of poverty, chastity, obedience in a stable state, CCC 944); SINGLE LIFE IN THE WORLD (affirmed in CCC 1658).
Off to the side, a separate bar labelled ORDINATION (bishop, priest, deacon) with an arrow marking that it is a sacrament, not a state of consecration, and that Latin deacons may be married.
A shaded box labelled LATIN DISCIPLINE (CCC 1579): priests and bishops normally celibate — marked 'changeable in principle, argued on fittingness'.
A second shaded box labelled EASTERN DISCIPLINE (CCC 1580): married men may be ordained deacons and priests; bishops are celibate — marked 'long-standing and legitimate'.

A decision gate at the bottom: 'Could a competent authority change this tomorrow without retracting a claim belonging to revelation? Yes = discipline; No = doctrine', with two output arrows labelled accordingly.

lessons.title: Creation care: the human vocation inside a created order that belongs to God
lessons.explanation: Objective: distinguish three kinds of claim in Catholic teaching on the environment — what creation is, what human dominion means, and what any particular policy should do — and to know which of the three an encyclical actually settles. Begin with the scriptural frame, in which the human being is placed in a garden "to till it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15), not handed a warehouse. The Catechism draws the limit from that: the dominion granted by the Creator over mineral, vegetable and animal resources "is not absolute; it is limited by concern for the quality of life of his neighbour, including generations to come" (CCC 2415), and it repeats the point in a second place so that it cannot be missed — that dominion "cannot be separated from respect for moral obligations, including those toward generations to come" (CCC 2456). The basis is not utility but creation's own goodness: "Each creature possesses its own particular goodness and perfection ... Man must therefore respect the particular goodness of every creature, to avoid any disordered use of things which would be in contempt of the Creator and would bring disastrous consequences for human beings and their environment" (CCC 339). CCC 340 adds the interdependence of creatures as willed by God, and CCC 2416–2418 sets the boundaries of the animal question precisely: animals are God's creatures and "men owe them kindness", using them for food, clothing and scientific research is legitimate "if it remains within reasonable limits", while it is "contrary to human dignity to cause animals to suffer or die needlessly" and unworthy to spend on them money that should relieve human misery. Those paragraphs are important because they cut against two opposite oversimplifications at once: they forbid treating creation as mere raw material, and they forbid collapsing the difference between animals and persons. Laudato Si' then extends the frame in a direction that has proved the most consequential in practice. Its chapter on the human roots of the crisis attacks what it calls the throwaway culture and treats the environmental question as inseparable from the question of the poor — the phrase "integral ecology" names that refusal to separate them (LS 10–11, 137–142). On the empirical side the encyclical states its judgement carefully: "A very solid scientific consensus indicates that we are presently witnessing a disturbing warming of the climatic system", while immediately conceding that "a scientifically determinable cause cannot be assigned to each particular phenomenon" (LS 23) — a sentence worth quoting precisely, because it shows the encyclical making an evidential judgement rather than a definition. The climate, it adds, is "a common good, belonging to all and meant for all" (LS 23), and the common good extends to those who come after us, so that "we can no longer speak of sustainable development apart from intergenerational solidarity" (LS 159). Crucially, the encyclical names its own limits: "the Church does not presume to settle scientific questions or to replace politics" (LS 188). That sentence is the hinge of this lesson. Catholic doctrine teaches that creation belongs to God, that its goods are destined for all, that the vulnerable and the unborn generations have claims on us, and that waste and contempt for creatures are moral failures. It does not teach which energy technology, which tax, which international agreement, or which growth rate is correct; those are argued by citizens and experts, and Catholics disagree about them legitimately. A critic who says the encyclical overreaches into contested science and economics is making an argument about the kind of claim being made, and the answer is not to deny that the encyclical contains empirical judgements — it does, and judgements of that kind are held with the assent proper to non-definitive teaching and remain open to revision as evidence changes.
lessons.example: Work a parish dispute through the analysis, because the disputes are where the distinctions earn their keep. A parish council is asked to spend a large sum on building fabric and receives two proposals: replace an ageing gas boiler with an electric heat pump at significant cost, and divest the parish's small reserve fund from fossil-fuel index funds at some loss of income to the parish's charitable giving. Four claims are now on the table and they must be sorted before anyone argues. Claim one, doctrinal: creation belongs to God and must be treated with respect rather than exploited without limit (CCC 2415, 2456), and the goods of the earth are destined for all, including the poor and future generations (LS 159). This claim is not negotiable and it rules out one framing in advance — the framing that says the environment is a purely private preference with no moral content. Claim two, empirical: whether the heat pump will in fact reduce the parish's emissions given the local grid's generation mix, and over what payback period. This is a question for engineers and utility data; the moral teaching does not answer it, and a parish that skips the calculation has confused zeal with prudence. Claim three, prudential about means: whether the money is better spent on the boiler, on a refugee-housing contribution, or on nothing while the roof is repaired. Here the doctrine gives real constraints — the poor have a claim, waste is wrong, and the roof protects actual people — but it does not rank these options for you. Claim four, ecclesial-political: whether divestment is a fitting public witness or an empty gesture that costs the parish's charity. Catholics argue this both ways and both are arguing inside the tradition. Note the diagnostic. The question "is creation care a Catholic obligation?" was settled long before Laudato Si'; the question "should this parish buy a heat pump?" is not a doctrinal question at all, and it is answered by a mixture of data, cost, and judgement about priorities, for which the parish is accountable but not infallible. A learner who can say which of the four claims is which has learned more than a learner who has memorised a slogan, in either direction.
lessons.question: A commentator says that since Laudato Si' is an encyclical, Catholics are bound to support the specific climate policies the Pope recommends in it, such as carbon pricing. Which assessment is accurate?
lessons.answer: The encyclical teaches doctrine about creation, the common good and intergenerational justice, but it also states its own limit — that the Church 'does not presume to settle scientific questions or to replace politics' (LS 188) — so its particular policy recommendations are prudential judgements that Catholics may weigh and dispute.
lessons.distractor: The commentator is right: all the pope's specific policy proposals in an encyclical are binding teaching, and dissent from them is dissent from the Church's social doctrine.
lessons.correction: Two different objects of assent are in play. The doctrinal claims — that creation is God's and has its own goodness (CCC 339, 2415), that the goods of the earth are destined for all, that the common good reaches future generations (LS 159) — are taught and bind. The particular policy instruments proposed in the encyclical are prudential judgements about contingent matters: the encyclical itself says the Church does not presume to settle scientific questions or to replace politics (LS 188), and it concedes that a scientifically determinable cause cannot be assigned to each particular phenomenon (LS 23). So respect for the document requires recognising the weight of its moral teaching while leaving room to argue about mechanisms; accusing a Catholic who prefers a different instrument of dissent from doctrine misdescribes the act. Note the mirror error, also common: treating the whole encyclical as opinion, which would ignore that its moral claims are acts of the ordinary magisterium and part of the social teaching.

depth.definitions: Integral ecology: the encyclical's term for an approach that refuses to treat environmental questions separately from social ones — "an integral ecology lived out joyfully and authentically", named in relation to St Francis of Assisi (LS 10–11), developed through economics, culture and daily life. Common good: the sum of social conditions allowing people to reach fulfilment more fully and more easily (CCC 1906), which LS 159 extends across generations. Dominion: the mandate of Genesis 1:26–28, read by the Catechism as real but limited, "by concern for the quality of life of his neighbour, including generations to come" (CCC 2415), and "not absolute". Throwaway culture: LS's name for a mentality that treats persons, things and relationships as disposable (LS 20–22). Intergenerational solidarity: the claim that duties reach those who cannot yet reciprocate, grounded in the world as gift (LS 159). Ordinary magisterium: teaching that binds without being a definition; social encyclicals belong here, and their contingent judgements are held with the assent proper to that mode. Intrinsic goodness of creatures: the claim that creatures are good because God wills and sustains them (CCC 339–340), which grounds duties toward them that are not derived from their usefulness to us. Limits of competence: the explicit statement that the Church does not settle scientific questions or replace politics (LS 188).
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that makes this tractable is the distinction between the moral frame and the empirical content, and it can be stated as a three-part test. Part one asks whose good is at stake: if a proposed action treats creation as pure means without remainder, or wastes what is destined for all, it contradicts the frame and no amount of policy cleverness rescues it (CCC 2415, 2456). Part two asks whether the claim about the world is empirical. If a document asserts that a warming trend is real or that a causal factor predominates, that assertion is about contingent evidence and has the epistemic status of evidence: it is to be taken seriously, especially when it carries the weight of an act of the magisterium, but it is also revisable if the evidence changes, which is precisely why the encyclical's own hedging language matters. Part three asks who is competent. If the question is which technology, tariff or treaty is wisest, the competence lies with the relevant expertise and the political community, and the Church's role is to specify constraints — protection of the poor, no gratuitous harm, no exclusion of the unborn generations — rather than to select the instrument. This three-part test also explains a frequent pattern in disputes: the same sentence in an encyclical gets quoted by one side as doctrine and by the other as opinion, and the disagreement is usually about which part of the sentence is which. Comparing 2415 with 188 makes the mix visible in a single lesson: the first is a norm, the second is an act of institutional self-limitation.
depth.secondExample: Shift the same instrument to a different environmental case where the moral and the technical interlock in a way that surprises learners: animal agriculture and diet. CCC 2417 permits the use of animals for food and clothing, so a claim that Catholic doctrine requires vegetarianism is false; but CCC 2418 forbids causing animals "to suffer or die needlessly" and criticises spending on animals money that should relieve human misery, so an industrial practice defended purely by price is not thereby justified either. Then add the Laudato Si' layer, which treats food waste, agricultural emissions and the claims of the hungry as one problem; and then add the genuinely contested layer, which is what a household or a nation should do about it — whether to reduce meat consumption, how much, at what cost to livelihoods, and with what transition arrangements for farmers. The pattern is identical to the parish boiler case: a real moral norm, real empirical questions, and an instrument question that faithful Catholics answer differently. Notice how much clearer the argument becomes when a disputant is asked to label each sentence of their own case, and how much of the heat in environmental disputes comes from people labelling the empirical as doctrinal and the doctrinal as merely political.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error is category substitution in one of two directions. Direction one, policy-as-doctrine: asserting that the encyclical's prudential proposals bind, so that a Catholic with a different energy policy is accused of rejecting Church teaching. This is answered by LS 188 and by the ordinary-magisterium treatment of contingent judgements. Direction two, doctrine-as-preference: asserting that environmental concern is a private taste, that creation has value only as a resource, or that concern for the climate is incompatible with concern for the poor — a framing that contradicts CCC 2415 and 2456 directly, and that LS 137–142 addresses by identifying the poor as the first victims of ecological degradation. A third, subtler mistake is the opposite of both: treating "integral ecology" as a ready-made policy platform rather than as a way of refusing to separate questions, so that the term becomes a label rather than an instrument. Diagnostic: ask the learner to state which part of their claim would survive if the empirical evidence changed, and which part would not. If nothing would change, they have mistaken the empirical for the doctrinal; if everything would, they have mistaken the doctrinal for the empirical.
depth.application: Task: the four-claim sorting exercise, written up as one page, applied to an environmental decision inside an institution you know (a parish, school, workplace or household — no personal or pastoral details about identifiable people). Produce: (1) DOCTRINAL — two claims from Scripture or the Catechism that constrain the decision, each with a paragraph reference; (2) EMPIRICAL — two factual claims that must be checked before deciding, with a note on what evidence would establish each; (3) PRUDENTIAL — the decision itself, stated as a choice between at least two means, with one sentence of reasoning for the option you favour and one sentence for the strongest argument against it; (4) SELF-LIMITING — one sentence modelled on the encyclical's own concession about what the Church does not presume to settle, applied to your own case, naming who has competence. Self-review rubric: full credit requires that the doctrinal claims are ones the Church actually teaches and are cited; that the empirical claims are genuinely checkable and are not smuggled moral assertions; that the prudential section states the opposite case in its strongest form rather than a caricature; and that no sentence accuses those who disagree with your preference of dissent from Catholic doctrine. A paper that makes the decision sound obvious, or that never names a counter-argument, has failed on the third criterion regardless of its conclusion.
depth.summary: Keep three things in one frame. Creation is God's and is good in itself, so dominion is stewardship with limits, and those limits reach to the neighbour, to the poor and to generations not yet born (CCC 339, 2415, 2456). Human work is the way the garden is tilled, so the theology of creation and the theology of work are the same theology seen from two sides (Genesis 2:15; LS 124–128; lesson 51). And the policies are ours to argue about, under constraints the Church does state and with expert judgement the Church explicitly does not claim to supply (LS 23, 188). Carry the same three-part sorting into the rest of this unit: lesson 56 turns it into a formal analysis of acts, lesson 57 asks how moral norms are actually derived rather than merely asserted, and lesson 60 will use it to weigh a contested policy question end to end, including a case where the doctrinal constraints and the prudential disagreement are unusually hard to keep apart.

readings.note: Read 23 for the climate as a common good along with the encyclical's own evidential caveat, 124–128 for work as the tilling of the garden, 159 for intergenerational solidarity, and — most important of all — 188, where the Church states that she does not presume to settle scientific questions or to replace politics.

readings.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church: the goodness of creatures and the seventh commandment's ecological content (CCC 339–341, 2415–2418, 2456)
readings.note: CCC 339–341 for the intrinsic goodness of creatures and their God-willed interdependence, 2415–2418 for the limits of dominion and the treatment of animals, 2456 for obligations toward future generations. Find paragraphs by number in the index.

readings.note: Read the four sections in order — biblical aspects; man and the universe of created things; the crisis in the relationship between man and the environment; a common responsibility, including the environment as a collective good and new lifestyles. It is the systematic version of the material the encyclicals argue.

readings.title: Benedict XVI, Caritas in Veritate (2009), 48–51

Useful for seeing continuity across pontificates and for the connection it draws between ecology and a distorted view of human nature.

readings.title: Sacred Scripture: Genesis, chapter 2 (USCCB New American Bible, with notes)
readings.note: The garden account, including 2:15 and the note on the human being's task of tilling and keeping. Read 2:4–25 rather than the whole chapter. Caveat: USCCB pages sometimes refuse automated clients with a 403 while loading normally in a browser; if a script cannot read it, open it in a browser.

visual.title: Sorting an environmental decision into its four kinds of claim
visual.description: A four-column sorting frame with a worked example legible in each column, and a decision gate that shows who has competence to settle each column.
steps: Top bar, labelled THE FRAME: 'The earth is the Lord's' — creation belongs to God and each creature is good in itself (CCC 339, 2415), with dominion limited by the neighbour and by future generations (CCC 2456).
Column 1, DOCTRINAL: claims taught by the Church, cited by paragraph — for example that creation has its own goodness and that its goods are destined for all.
Column 2, EMPIRICAL: checkable facts — for example the local grid's emissions intensity; marked 'evidence decides, and evidence can change'.
Column 3, PRUDENTIAL: the choice of means — heat pump or roof repair; marked 'Catholics may differ, and both may be faithful'.
Column 4, SELF-LIMIT: a box quoting LS 188, 'the Church does not presume to settle scientific questions or to replace politics', and naming who holds competence for each disputed item.
Decision gate at the base: 'Which column does your sentence belong in? If all three, state each part separately' — with an output arrow labelled 'no accidental excommunication of those who differ'.

questions.prompt: A company defends paying its warehouse staff a rate that leaves full-time workers below what is needed for housing and food, on the ground that the rate is the market clearing wage and every worker accepted it freely. Using the material from this unit, which analysis is correct?
questions.answer: The defence fails the norm: because the person is the subject of work, remuneration must sustain a dignified life for the worker and dependents (GS 67), and CCC 2434 states that to refuse or withhold a just wage can be a grave injustice, so the workers' consent does not repair the terms.
questions.distractor: The defence succeeds, because the Church teaches that wages are determined by the labour market and that a freely accepted contract settles the moral question.
questions.correction: The premise that free acceptance settles the question contradicts the material in lesson 51: the reason the Church speaks about wages at all is that the acting person is the subject and beneficiary of work (LE 6), and the council draws from that ranking both the right to work and remuneration that allows the worker to "cultivate worthily his own material, social, cultural, and spiritual life and that of his dependents" (GS 67). CCC 2434 treats withholding such a wage as a possible grave injustice, not as a market outcome beyond moral assessment. What the doctrine does not do is name the remedy: a minimum rate, sectoral bargaining, portable benefits and cooperative ownership are all instruments on which faithful Catholics may differ, and the correct conclusion is a floor plus duties, not a policy prescription.

questions.prompt: A couple married in the Church for eleven years separate, obtain a civil divorce, and one of them asks a parish catechist whether the marriage "no longer counts" now that the state has dissolved it. Which answer best reflects the Church's teaching?
questions.answer: A ratified and consummated marriage between baptized persons cannot be dissolved by any human authority, since the bond is established by God and the Church does not have the power to contravene that disposition (CCC 1640; GS 48), so the civil dissolution does not end it, though a tribunal may examine whether a valid marriage ever came into being.
questions.distractor: The civil dissolution ends the marriage in the Church's eyes as well, since the Church recognises the authority of the state over marriage contracts and the pastoral question is now simply one of a new union.
questions.correction: Lesson 52 separated three layers, and this question turns on keeping them apart. The bond is the bottom layer: CCC 1640 states that a marriage concluded and consummated between baptized persons can never be dissolved and that this results from God's disposition rather than from an ecclesiastical rule, which is why the honest answer to the couple is that no legal act ends it. The middle layer is the theology of marriage as a covenant signifying Christ's fidelity (FC 13; GS 48), which is argued rather than defined. The top layer is pastoral discipline, where the application of Amoris Laetitia 300-305 is genuinely contested and implemented differently. The distractor collapses the layers by treating the state's action as dissolving the bond, which is the error of confusing a changeable discipline with the bond itself, and it also skips the distinct canonical question of validity.

questions.prompt: A speaker tells a youth group that the Church's teaching about the body is defined doctrine because the pope delivered it in the theology of the body, and that the phrase "the nuptial meaning of the body" comes from Genesis. Which correction is accurate?
questions.answer: The catecheses are acts of the ordinary papal magisterium with real authority but not definitions; "the nuptial meaning of the body" is John Paul II's reading of Genesis 2:23-25 rather than a phrase of Scripture, and the doctrinal claims about marriage, chastity and the conjugal act stand on their own in the Catechism and in Gaudium et Spes.
questions.distractor: The speaker is right, since everything a pope teaches in general audiences is defined doctrine, and the nuptial meaning of the body is a revealed truth of Scripture.
questions.correction: Lesson 53's rule is to grade the act before arguing about the content. The Wednesday catecheses of 1979-1984 are ordinary magisterial teaching and carry real weight, but they are not definitions, so describing them as defined doctrine inflates the act; and "the nuptial meaning of the body", which appears in the audience of 6 February 1980, is the pope's interpretation of Genesis 2:23-25, not the words of the sacred text, which the USCCB edition shows plainly. The correction has a second half worth stating: deflating these catecheses to mere devotion is an equal error, because they articulate the anthropology that texts such as Familiaris Consortio 13 presuppose. What is taught independently of the catecheses is the doctrinal content in CCC 1601, 2337 and 2360-2361.

questions.prompt: A young Catholic is told that he cannot be considered serious about his faith if he does not support abolishing the discipline of priestly celibacy, because the discipline is merely human and married clergy in the Eastern Catholic Churches show the Latin rule is a mistake. Which assessment of the argument is correct?
questions.answer: The premise that celibacy is a discipline rather than a doctrine is correct (CCC 1579-1580), which makes the question legitimately arguable, but the conclusion that a Catholic must support abolition does not follow, since a changeable discipline still calls for a judgement of fittingness and no doctrine requires that judgement to go one way.
questions.distractor: The argument is correct in both parts: because celibacy is only a discipline, a Catholic who does not work for its abolition is being inconsistent with the Church's own recognition of married Eastern clergy.
questions.correction: Lesson 54 taught a two-part test: a rule is discipline if a competent authority could change it without retracting a claim belonging to revelation. Celibacy in the Latin Church passes that test, as CCC 1580 shows in stating that a different discipline has been in force in the Eastern Churches for centuries and that married men can be ordained there as deacons and priests, a practice "long considered legitimate". But a changeable rule is not thereby a defective one, and Paul VI's Sacerdotalis Caelibatus defends it with arguments from fittingness and sign-value. So the honest position has two halves: the question is genuinely open, and no Catholic is obliged to conclude that the discipline should be abolished. The distractor's error is the commonest one in this area, converting a legitimate argument into a test of loyalty.

questions.prompt: A diocese issues a teaching note saying that because the Church teaches the earth is God's, Catholics are bound in conscience to support a specific carbon tax bill. Using the unit's material, which response is best?
questions.answer: The note overstates the act: the doctrinal claims about creation, the universal destination of goods and intergenerational justice bind (CCC 339, 2415, 2456; LS 159), but the encyclical itself says the Church does not presume to settle scientific questions or to replace politics (LS 188), so a particular tax is a prudential proposal that Catholics may support, reject or modify.
questions.distractor: The note is correct, because an encyclical's specific policy recommendations are part of the Church's social doctrine and carry the same authority as its moral principles.
questions.correction: Lesson 55's four-column sorting applies directly. Column one contains taught norms: creation has its own goodness, dominion is limited by the neighbour and by future generations, and goods are destined for all. Column two contains empirical claims, including the encyclical's own careful statement that a very solid consensus indicates a disturbing warming while a scientifically determinable cause cannot be assigned to each particular phenomenon (LS 23). Column three contains prudential choices about means, which is where a carbon tax lives, and column four is the Church's own self-limitation in LS 188. Treating the third column as though it were the first accuses Catholics who prefer a different instrument of dissent from doctrine, which is the opposite error to treating the whole encyclical as mere opinion.

units.title: Moral Method and the Contested Cases: From the Object of the Act to a Prudential Judgement

lessons.title: Object, intention and circumstance: why consequences alone cannot settle a case
lessons.explanation: Objective: name the three sources of the morality of a human act, explain what each one does, and say precisely why the third cannot override the first. The Catechism states the list in one sentence: "The morality of human acts depends on: the object chosen; the end in view or the intention; the circumstances of the action. The object, the intention, and the circumstances make up the 'sources,' or constitutive elements, of the morality of human acts" (CCC 1750). Each term then gets a definition. The object "is a good toward which the will deliberately directs itself. It is the matter of a human act", and it is the object that "morally specifies the act of the will" (CCC 1751). The intention "resides in the acting subject" and "is an element essential to the moral evaluation" because it determines the act by its end (CCC 1752) — but it cannot rescue a bad object: "A good intention ... does not make behavior that is intrinsically disordered, such as lying and calumny, good or just. The end does not justify the means", while an added bad intention can make an otherwise good act — almsgiving for vainglory — evil (CCC 1753). The circumstances, "including the consequences, are secondary elements of a moral act. They contribute to increasing or diminishing the moral goodness or evil of human acts ... They can also diminish or increase the agent's responsibility ... Circumstances of themselves cannot change the moral quality of acts themselves; they can make neither good nor right an action that is in itself evil" (CCC 1754). Finally the whole: "A morally good act requires the goodness of the object, of the end, and of the circumstances together" (CCC 1755). Veritatis Splendor tightens one term that learners always loosen. The object is "not ... a process or an event of the merely physical order, to be assessed on the basis of its ability to bring about a given state of affairs in the outside world. Rather, that object is the proximate end of a deliberate decision" (VS 78) — so the moral analysis is done from the perspective of the acting person and from what she is choosing, not from a description of the physics. From that the encyclical draws the conclusion that there are acts "incapable of being ordered" to God, "intrinsically evil (intrinsece malum): they are such always and per se ... quite apart from the ulterior intentions of the one acting and the circumstances" (VS 80), and it rejects the thesis "characteristic of teleological and proportionalist theories" that no act can be graded evil in its species apart from intention or the totality of foreseeable consequences (VS 79). Fair statement of the rejected position: its Catholic proponents argued that goods are many and finite, that moral norms about material acts are reliable but not absolute, and that the right judgement weighs the pre-moral goods and evils at stake in a situation. They were not relativists; several taught that some acts are virtually never justified. Veritatis Splendor answers that such a weighing cannot ground exceptionless negative norms and that this "cannot claim to be grounded in the Catholic moral tradition" (VS 76). Aquinas supplies a precision the modern debate usually loses. On whether consequences increase the goodness or malice of an act, he distinguishes foreseen from unforeseen: consequences that are foreseen "increase the goodness or malice", because foreseeing evils and not removing them is itself part of what is chosen (ST I–II q.20 a.5). So consequences are not irrelevant; they enter through foresight and intention, and they can aggravate or mitigate, which is exactly the Catechism's "secondary elements" — not the primary determinant of the species. Reading the three sources this way also gives the correct diagnosis of the common slogan "the end justifies the means", which is false, and of its equally common opposite "intentions are all that matter", which is also false.
lessons.example: Take the case that made the distinction famous and then a modern one. First the classical case, because Aquinas analyses it himself. A man is attacked and repels the attacker; the blow kills. Aquinas grants that the one act "may have two effects, one is the saving of one's life, the other is the slaying of the aggressor", and holds the act lawful because "one's intention is to save one's own life", adding the formulation that later tradition built on: "Nothing hinders one act from having two effects, only one of which is intended, while the other is beside the intention", and that "moral acts take their species according to what is intended, and not according to what is beside the intention" (ST II–II q.64 a.7). Note that he adds a proportionality condition in the same article — if a man in self-defence uses more violence than necessary, "it will be unlawful" — which is why the later four-condition formulation of double effect includes both proportionality and the requirement that the bad effect not be the means to the good one. Now the modern case, so that you can run the analysis yourself. A physician caring for a dying patient whose pain is not controlled gives escalating doses of an opioid, knowing that the dose may depress respiration and shorten life. Sort the sources. The object, stated as the acting person's proximate end, is the relief of pain by analgesia — a good object, not "the killing of the patient". The intention is the relief of suffering, not the death; this is why the Catechism can say that the use of painkillers to alleviate the sufferings of the dying "even at the risk of shortening their days, can be morally in conformity with human dignity if death is not willed as either an end or a means, but only foreseen and tolerated as inevitable" (CCC 2279). The circumstances — the dose, the titration, the availability of palliative alternatives, the patient's consent — bear on the goodness of the act and on culpability, and gross negligence in the circumstances can wreck an otherwise good act. Now change one element and watch the analysis flip: the same physician administers a lethal dose with the purpose of ending the patient's life because the suffering is unbearable. The object has changed, not the consequences: the proximate end chosen is the patient's death, and the good intention of ending suffering does not rescue it, because the death is now the means "chosen precisely to end the suffering" — which is what CCC 2277 calls direct euthanasia, "an act or omission which, of itself or by intention, causes death in order to eliminate suffering". Notice what the example rules out at both ends: a proportionalist who said the two cases are morally equivalent because the outcomes are similar has dissolved the object; and a rigorist who said the opioid case is simply euthanasia has ignored intention and the principle that consequences may be foreseen without being intended. Both errors come from using one of the three sources as if it were the only one.
lessons.question: A manager defends ordering an employee to falsify a safety report by arguing that the plant will otherwise be shut down and many families will lose income. Which analysis is correct?
lessons.answer: The act fails at the object: deliberate falsification of a report in a matter affecting others' safety is intrinsically disordered, so a good intention cannot make it right — the end does not justify the means (CCC 1753) — though the circumstances of pressure may reduce culpability.
lessons.distractor: The act may be justified by the proportion of goods and harms: preventing the loss of many incomes outweighs the wrong of a false report, so the manager's reasoning is morally sound.
lessons.correction: Two moves combine to license the manager. First, the object has been described only physically as 'writing on a form' rather than as what is chosen: a false report on a safety matter, which is the proximate end of the decision (VS 78). Second, the circumstances and consequences have been promoted from secondary elements (CCC 1754) to the decisive criterion, which is precisely the thesis of the teleological and proportionalist theories that VS 79 rejects: that an act cannot be graded evil in its species apart from the intention or the totality of foreseeable consequences. The good intention does not convert the object (CCC 1753). Two things are worth saying next: the circumstances — duress, threat of closure — are morally relevant to culpability and should be weighed (CCC 1754), and the manager's underlying worry about livelihoods is a genuine good that must be pursued by other means, for example by escalating the hazard through proper channels. So the correction is not 'the manager is a bad person' but 'the offered justification is not the right kind of reason'.

depth.definitions: Object: the good toward which the will deliberately directs itself; the matter of the act, and what morally specifies it (CCC 1751); not the physical event but "the proximate end of a deliberate decision" (VS 78). Intention or end: the movement of the will toward the goal of the activity, residing in the acting subject and essential to evaluation (CCC 1752). Circumstances: the features of the situation including consequences, secondary elements that can increase or diminish goodness and responsibility but cannot change the species (CCC 1754). Sources of morality: the three together (CCC 1750). Intrinsic evil (intrinsece malum): an act incapable of being ordered to God by reason of its object, always and per se, apart from ulterior intentions and circumstances (VS 80). Proportionalism or teleologism: the family of theories that judges the rightness of an act by weighing the pre-moral goods and evils involved, and that the Church rejects as unable to ground exceptionless negative norms (VS 74–79). Double effect: the analysis that permits an act with one good and one bad effect when the bad effect is not intended, is not the means to the good, and is proportionate — historically rooted in Aquinas's treatment of self-defence (ST II–II q.64 a.7) and reflected in CCC 2279. Foreseen versus unintended consequences: at ST I–II q.20 a.5, consequences that are foreseen enter the moral character of the act; those that are not foreseen do not.
depth.mechanism: Why does the object get priority rather than the outcome? The Catechism's answer is about persons: acts are moral because they "express and determine the goodness or evil of the individual who performs them", shaping "his profound spiritual traits" (VS 71). If outcomes were decisive, the agent's own choice would drop out of the analysis — a person would be assessed as a producer of states of affairs rather than as one who chooses goods, and the very thing the Church says makes an act moral, the deliberation and consent of the acting person, would be graded last. That is the argument, and it explains the structure of the three sources as a dependency chain rather than a checklist. The object specifies what kind of act this is; the intention specifies why it is done; the circumstances specify how and in what situation. Only when all three are good is the act good (CCC 1755), and a defect in the object is not repairable upstream, which is why the Catechism says the object "can by itself vitiate an act in its entirety" (CCC 1755). Now the counter-argument, stated in its strongest form, because you will meet it: the proportionalist says that every finite good can conflict with another finite good, that the object cannot be described morally without reference to what is at stake, and that a hard line on objects produces absurdities — a rule that forbids a small harm to prevent a catastrophe. The Church's reply is partly conceptual (the description of the object is not arbitrary; it is the proximate end of the will) and partly practical (she claims the object-based account is what the tradition actually held, VS 76, and that it protects the weak by making some acts unthinkable as policy). The honest learner should be able to state both, and should notice the shared premise: both agree that consequences are morally relevant; they disagree about whether consequences can re-specify the object itself.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting pair from ordinary life, to show that the instrument is not only for dramatic cases. Case one: a salesperson gives a client an exaggerated but non-contractual impression of a product's durability. Case two: the same salesperson states a factual claim about durability that she believes after checking the test data, but which turns out to be wrong. Both cause the same harm to the buyer; the moral analyses diverge entirely. In the first, the object chosen is deception, and the intention of making a living does not repair it (CCC 1753); the circumstances might mitigate responsibility if the seller was pressured by a supervisor and had no real alternative, which is a judgement about culpability rather than about the act. In the second, the object is truthful communication; there is no bad object and no bad intention, and the harm is unintended and unforeseen-though-responsible, which raises questions of diligence and of reparation rather than of intrinsically disordered choice. The pair also exposes the mistake of grading acts by damage alone: identical damage, different acts. Now use the same pair to see where circumstances do real work: if in case one the seller works under a manager who threatens dismissal for any missed quota, the circumstances "can also diminish or increase the agent's responsibility" (CCC 1754) — the act remains wrong and the culpability may be small, which is exactly the pastoral distinction that lesson 52 encountered in a different setting.
depth.mistake: The two predictable errors are mirror images. Error one, consequentialism: "all that matters is the outcome" — refuted directly by CCC 1754 and VS 79–80, and identifiable in argument by the presence of a purely physical description of the act plus a comparison of net harms. Error two, a formalism that treats the three sources as a mechanical checklist and ignores that the object must be described from the acting person's perspective: this produces absurd verdicts, for example classifying a surgeon's incision as a mutilation or a life-saving vaccination as an assault, because the analysis has stopped at the physical event rather than the proximate end of the choice (VS 78). A third error, common in pastoral and medical discussions, is the attempt to justify a directly intended evil as "double effect" when the evil is in fact the means: if the death of the patient, or the death of the unborn child, is what is used to secure the benefit, the conditions for double effect fail at the second condition, and the appeal to proportion does not save it. Diagnostic to teach: ask the learner to write one sentence beginning "what the agent is choosing, as her proximate end, is ..." If that sentence names a good, the analysis proceeds; if it names an evil, no consideration of consequences or intention will make the act good, though it may make the person less culpable.
depth.application: Task: a structured moral analysis of one case you construct yourself, of roughly 700 words, with the following mandated headings. (1) NARRATIVE: two or three sentences of concrete situation, with no identifying details about real people. (2) OBJECT: one sentence on the proximate end of the agent's choice, deliberately worded so it would not apply to the same physical behaviour done for a different end. (3) INTENTION: what the agent aims at, and one statement of what she does not aim at. (4) CIRCUMSTANCES: three features of the situation, and for each, one clause saying whether it bears on the act's goodness, on culpability, or on both. (5) VERDICT: whether the act is good, evil, or good-with-attendant-bad-effect, naming the source that decides the verdict. (6) THE OTHER SIDE: the strongest argument a proportionalist would make against your verdict, in two sentences, followed by one sentence saying why you do not accept it. Self-review rubric: the analysis passes if the object sentence meets the test of being end-specific; if no verdict rests on consequences alone; if circumstances are correctly described as secondary; and if the proportionalist case is stated in a form its own advocate would accept rather than as a straw figure. An analysis that never states the opposing case, or that reaches a verdict by arithmetic on harms, is not yet at the required standard. Note the standing caveat: retrieval questions and written exercises can test whether you can run the analysis, but they cannot certify the prudence or the virtue required to make such judgements in real lives.
depth.summary: The three sources are a dependency chain, not a checklist: the object specifies the act, the intention specifies the agent's aim, the circumstances specify the situation and affect culpability, and only their joint goodness makes the act good (CCC 1750, 1755). Consequences are real and morally relevant — foreseen ones aggravate or diminish (ST I–II q.20 a.5; CCC 1754) — but they cannot change the species of an act or convert an intrinsically disordered choice into a good one (CCC 1754; VS 80), which is why the correct analysis of a hard case begins by writing down what the agent is choosing rather than what the world will look like afterwards. Transfer the instrument immediately: it is the analytical core of lesson 57, where the derivation of the norms that specify objects is examined, and of lesson 59, where withholding disproportionate treatment, intending pain relief that may shorten life, and intending a patient's death must be separated, since the Church's teaching treats the first two as legitimate in principle and the third as absolutely excluded (CCC 2277–2279).

visual.title: The three sources of a moral act, as a dependency chain
visual.description: A three-stage pipeline in which the object gates the act, the intention supplies the agent's aim, and the circumstances adjust goodness and culpability but cannot rewrite the first stage.
steps: Stage 1, OBJECT (CCC 1751; VS 78): write the agent's proximate end in one end-specific sentence. Label 'this specifies the act and cannot be repaired later'.
Gate symbol beneath stage 1: if the object is an intrinsically disordered choice, the chain is closed — marked 'no amount of intention or consequence opens this gate' (CCC 1754; VS 80).
Stage 2, INTENTION (CCC 1752): write the agent's aim and, separately, what she does not aim at. Label 'a good intention cannot convert a bad object; a bad intention can spoil a good one' (CCC 1753).
Stage 3, CIRCUMSTANCES (CCC 1754): list three features of the situation, splitting each into 'affects the goodness of the act' or 'affects culpability'.
A parallel lane labelled CONSEQUENCES, entering between stage 2 and stage 3 with the rule from ST I–II q.20 a.5: foreseen consequences aggravate or diminish; unforeseen ones do not enter here.
Output box: 'A morally good act requires the goodness of the object, of the end and of the circumstances together' (CCC 1755) — with a warning tab reading 'consequences alone do not settle a case'.

lessons.title: Natural law: how the argument actually runs, and how it is actually attacked
lessons.explanation: Objective: be able to reconstruct the natural-law argument in its own terms rather than reciting its conclusion, and to state the standard objections fairly enough that their advocates would recognise them. The argument has four moving parts. First, law is defined functionally: it "is nothing else than an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated" (Aquinas, ST I–II q.90 a.4), and it is promulgated to the natural law's subjects "by the very fact that God instilled it into man's mind so as to be known by him naturally" (same article, reply 1). Second, the natural law is not a separate code but a participation: "this participation of the eternal law in the rational creature is called the natural law", so that "the natural law is nothing else than the rational creature's participation of the eternal law" (ST I–II q.91 a.2). Third, the content is derived from goods: "the first precept of law" is "that good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided. All other precepts of the natural law are based upon this: so that whatever the practical reason naturally apprehends as man's good (or evil) belongs to the precepts of the natural law" (ST I–II q.94 a.2), and the precepts stand to practical reason as the first principles of demonstration stand to speculative reason. Fourth, and most important for how the argument is actually argued, the derivation weakens as it descends: the practical reason "is busied with contingent matters ... and consequently, although there is necessity in the general principles, the more we descend to matters of detail, the more frequently we encounter defects" (ST I–II q.94 a.4). The Catechism states the same structure in modern form: the natural law "expresses the original moral sense which enables man to discern by reason the good and the evil" (CCC 1954); it "states the first and essential precepts which govern the moral life" and hinges on the desire for God and on "the sense that the other is one's equal" (CCC 1955); it is "universal in its precepts and its authority extends to all men" (CCC 1956); it is "immutable and permanent throughout the variations of history" in the sense that "the rules that express it remain substantially valid" even when "rejected in its very principles" (CCC 1958); and it grounds civil law (CCC 1959). The Catechism also concedes the epistemic problem honestly: "The precepts of natural law are not perceived by everyone clearly and immediately" (CCC 1960). Veritatis Splendor's chapter on this is where the argument becomes contested in practice, because it insists that there are negative norms "which oblige without exception" (VS 76, 82) and rejects the view that universal moral norms cannot be formulated across cultures (VS 43–45, 50–53). Now the objections, stated as their advocates would state them. Objection one, the derivation problem: from a description of what human beings are and tend toward, it does not follow without further premises what they ought to do — the classic is/ought gap, and natural-law theorists must show the bridge rather than assume it. Objection two, an internal family quarrel about method: one school derives norms by attending to the basic human goods intelligible in themselves (the "new natural law" associated with Germain Grisez and John Finnis), while a more traditional reading works from natural inclinations in the manner of Aquinas's q.94 a.2; the two can reach different verdicts, so "natural law" does not name one settled method. Objection three, the theological objection: some Protestant theologians, following Barth, argue that a natural moral knowledge available apart from revelation and grace compromises the sufficiency of Scripture and the necessity of grace — a position the Catholic reply locates in a different doctrine of nature and grace rather than in a lesser concern for Scripture. Objection four, the critical objection: that appeals to "nature" have repeatedly encoded contingent social arrangements, so that natural-law language functions as a way to make contested arrangements look necessary. The Catholic response to the last two is not a denial that the language has been abused but a distinction between an argument's content and its misuse. What is not disputable, if you accept the Church's teaching at all, is that some moral knowledge is available to reason as such, which is what makes the Church's public argument with non-believers possible in the first place (VS 43–45).
lessons.example: Reconstruct one derivation from first principles to a specific norm, then mark exactly where the controversy enters. Start with the first precept: good is to be done and pursued, evil avoided (ST I–II q.94 a.2). This is not an inference but the form of practical reasoning: it is what an agent is already committed to in deliberating at all. Next, identify the goods the practical reason "naturally apprehends": life and health; knowledge; friendship and family; work and the shaping of the world; and, on the Church's reading, the good of religion and the beatific end to which all these are ordered (CCC 1955, and compare the list in q.94 a.2, which proceeds from self-preservation to the specifically rational goods). Next, note the bridge premise that the tradition inserts rather than hides: these goods are not merely facts about desire, they are perfections of the person, and reason grasps them as worth pursuing, which is why the derivation is not from "is" to "ought" but from "is a good" to "ought to be pursued", with the first precept supplying the connecting principle. That is the point where objection one presses hardest, and where the "new natural law" school would prefer to say the goods are self-evident to practical reason without appeal to inclinations at all. Now take a concrete norm and watch the derivation's strength vary with distance from the principles. The prohibition of deliberately killing an innocent human being sits close to the principles — the good of life is one of the first apprehended goods — and Aquinas's own treatment of self-defence shows how tight the reasoning is at that level (lesson 56). Move one level down to norms about property, wages, or the proper distribution of taxation, and the reasoning becomes what q.94 a.4 predicts: the general principle holds without fail, but the descent to detail "encounters defects" and reasonable people disagree, which is why the Church argues some of these as prudential matters. Finally, look at a genuinely contested case: the morality of capital punishment. The Church's teaching that the death penalty is inadmissible in the present circumstances rests on the dignity of the person and on a judgement about whether states actually need it, and that second part is contingent and argued (CCC 2267's own reasoning notes the development), which shows the same gradient inside a single paragraph. The lesson's practical payoff is that a natural-law argument must be executed with this gradient in view; the commonest abuse of the tradition is to present the conclusion with the certainty of the first precept while quietly skipping the descent.
lessons.question: A student rejects the natural law by observing that many people sincerely disagree about what is natural, and that some past appeals to nature served oppressive arrangements. Which response is most accurate to the Catholic position?
lessons.answer: Both observations can be granted without refuting the position: the Church herself says the precepts of natural law are not perceived by everyone clearly and immediately (CCC 1960) and that a general principle remains valid even when rejected or misapplied, so abuse and disagreement are problems of application and knowledge rather than evidence that no natural moral knowledge exists.
lessons.distractor: The observations refute natural law: if reasonable people disagree about a norm, that proves the norm is a cultural construction rather than something written into human nature.
lessons.correction: The inference 'people disagree, therefore no objective norm' does not follow in any domain: it would abolish arithmetic if some people counted badly. Aquinas anticipates the objection directly — the general principles are the same for all and known to all, but the descent to detail encounters defects, and practical reason deals with contingent matters (ST I–II q.94 a.4, a.6), and the Catechism restates the epistemic limit at CCC 1960. The historical charge of abuse is also better handled by conceding it than by denying it: appeals to nature have been used to defend oppression, and the response is to test the argument rather than to abandon the enterprise, especially because the Church's public moral argument with those who do not share her faith depends on there being some moral knowledge available to reason as such. Note the limit on the correct claim: this does not show that any particular derivation succeeds, and objectors are entitled to attack specific derivations, including the two lines of internal disagreement identified in the definitions above.

depth.definitions: Natural law: the rational creature's participation in the eternal law, "an imprint on us of the Divine light", by which reason discerns good and evil (Aquinas, ST I–II q.91 a.2). Eternal law: God's own ordinance of things to their end. First precept of practical reason: "good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided" (q.94 a.2), the formal principle of all further precepts. Self-evident in itself and self-evident to us: Aquinas's distinction between propositions evident from their terms and those that become evident to a learner (q.94 a.2). Basic goods: the human goods the practical reason naturally apprehends as ends worth pursuing — life, knowledge, friendship, work, and (on the Church's reading) religion and beatitude. Synderesis: the habitual grasp of the first principles of practical reason, discussed in q.94 a.1. Promulgation: the publication that gives a law its force; for the natural law this is God's instilling it in the human mind (q.90 a.4). Is/ought gap: the objection that value cannot be derived from fact without a further premise. New natural law: the twentieth-century school (Grisez, Finnis and others) that grounds practical reason's first principles in self-evident basic goods rather than in natural inclinations. Hierarchy of principle and application: the claim that general principles hold without fail while detailed norms involve contingent judgement (q.94 a.4).
depth.mechanism: The mechanism of a natural-law argument is a four-step descent, and the intellectual honesty of the argument consists in labelling which step you are on. Step one, the formal principle: good is to be pursued, evil avoided. Step two, the enumeration of goods: what counts as the human good — this step is where the schools divide, since the traditional reading appeals to natural inclinations and the newer reading appeals to self-evident practical truths, and the verdicts can differ. Step three, the specification of norms: the derivation of prohibitions and requirements from the goods, for example the derivation of the norm against deliberately killing the innocent from the good of life, or norms about marriage from the goods of fidelity and offspring (lesson 52). Step four, the application: judgements about this situation, this institution, this policy — the level at which the traditional analysis says "the more we descend to matters of detail, the more frequently we encounter defects" (q.94 a.4). Now notice why the criticism lands differently at different levels. Objections about cultural variance and ideological abuse most often target step four, whereas the magisterial claim that something is "immutable and permanent" is about steps one and two and about the substantial validity of the rules that express them (CCC 1958). A critic who shows that a seventeenth-century application was shaped by its era has not touched steps one and two; a critic who can show that a purported basic good is not in fact a perfection of the person has. This is why the productive way to argue with natural-law claims is to attack the specific step rather than the whole edifice, and why the Church's own documents, including Veritatis Splendor 43–53, spend their energy defending the possibility of universal norms at step three rather than restating step one.
depth.secondExample: Test the four-step descent on a case where the Church's teaching is contested even among Catholics, so you can see the machinery rather than the conclusion: the provision of lethal assistance to a terminally ill person who requests it. Step one is not in dispute. Step two is where the crucial move happens: the good of life is claimed to be a basic good — not merely a preference most people have, but a perfection of the person that no other good can be traded against without remainder, because it is the condition of possessing any other good. Notice that this is the load-bearing premise, and it is exactly the premise that a sophisticated opponent attacks first, arguing that a life of unrelievable suffering no longer participates in the goods it exists to serve. Step three derives the norm: deliberate killing of the innocent is excluded in every case, and CCC 2277 and Evangelium Vitae 65 state the norm in that form. Step four handles the application: how pain is managed, whether treatment is disproportionate, what counts as ordinary care, and who decides — the level at which lesson 59 does its work, and where the Church's prohibition of euthanasia stands beside judgements she explicitly leaves to medicine and prudence. Now compare a completely different derivation at the same four steps, this time about truthfulness, and you will see that the structure is domain-general: the good of knowing and being known grounds a norm about not deceiving, and the applications — what to say to a dying patient, whether a politician must disclose an error — are where judgement, and often legitimate disagreement, live. A learner who can name the step at which an argument is located has the skill this lesson exists to teach, and it is the same skill lesson 60 uses to separate doctrinal constraint from prudential dispute.
depth.mistake: Three mistakes recur. The first is treating natural law as a code that can be consulted the way one consults a rule book, so that any difficult case is assumed to have a read-off answer; the tradition itself denies this at q.94 a.4 and the Catechism concedes the epistemic difficulty at CCC 1960. The second is the reverse: concluding from hard cases and from historical abuse that natural law is merely ideology. That conclusion requires attacking step two — showing that some supposed good is not a good or that the derivation does not follow — and the mere existence of bad arguments proves only that arguments can be bad. The third is using natural law as a rhetorical trump in public argument: asserting "it is against nature" as though the phrase settled a question, when the phrase is a label for a conclusion that has not yet been argued. The diagnostic here is simple and severe: if a speaker cannot state the good at stake, the derivation from the good to the norm, and the level of application at which they are arguing, they have not made a natural-law argument — they have announced one. That discipline is also the reason this course's earlier lessons on doctrinal modes (lesson 31) and on the sources of morality (lesson 56) precede this one: the argument is only as good as the claims it is built from and the act descriptions it uses.
depth.application: Task: construct one short natural-law argument, of about 600 words, on a question of your choosing from this list — whether an employer may require employees to work on a day the employee holds sacred; whether a government may impose a vaccine requirement; whether a family may withhold a burdensome treatment from a dying relative. Your paper must contain, clearly labelled: (1) the first precept applied — one sentence; (2) THE GOODS AT STAKE — at least three, with a sentence for each saying why it is a perfection of the person rather than merely a preference; (3) THE NORM — one sentence stating what is prohibited or required, in a form that could be stated without reference to this case; (4) THE DESCENT — two or three sentences locating your argument at the level of detail, stating which part of your conclusion depends on contingent facts; (5) THE STRONGEST OBJECTION — the objection that attacks your step-two premises, stated as its advocate would state it, with your response; (6) WHAT WOULD CHANGE YOUR MIND — one factual or conceptual development that would alter your conclusion. Self-review rubric: full credit requires that the goods are argued for rather than asserted; that the norm is stated at a level of generality consistent with the goods; that the contingent part of the conclusion is acknowledged; and that the objection is not a straw figure. A paper that asserts a norm without naming the good, or that treats a contentious application as if it were the first precept, has not yet reached the standard.
depth.summary: Natural law is an argument structure rather than a list: a formal first precept, an account of the goods, a derivation of norms, and an application that grows more defeasible as it descends (ST I–II q.90 a.4, q.91 a.2, q.94 a.2, a.4; CCC 1954–1960). The Church holds that some moral knowledge is available to reason as such, which is what makes her public argument possible, that the general principles hold without fail, and that detailed applications are the work of practical wisdom rather than of recitation (CCC 1958, 1960; VS 43–53). The position is genuinely contested, and the objections worth engaging are the derivation problem, the internal disagreement between the traditional and the newer natural-law methods, the theological objection from the sufficiency of revelation, and the historical charge that appeals to nature have served oppression. Carrying this forward: lesson 58 turns from the structure of norms to the formation of the person who judges, which is the answer to the question of how practical wisdom is acquired, and lesson 60 requires you to use both — stating the doctrinal constraint in natural-law terms and then acknowledging precisely how much of a policy question the argument leaves open.
