lessons.title: Virtue and habit: how character shapes what a person can see and do
lessons.explanation: Objective: state what a virtue is in the Catholic tradition, explain the mechanism by which habits shape moral judgement, and know what the modern empirical objection to virtue ethics claims and what it does not show. The Catechism's definitions are compact. "A virtue is an habitual and firm disposition to do the good. It allows the person not only to perform good acts, but to give the best of himself. The virtuous person tends toward the good with all his sensory and spiritual powers" (CCC 1803). Human virtues are then described as "firm attitudes, stable dispositions, habitual perfections of intellect and will that govern our actions, order our passions, and guide our conduct according to reason and faith", and the crucial qualification follows immediately: "The moral virtues are acquired by human effort. They are the fruit and seed of morally good acts" (CCC 1804). Four of them are cardinal because the moral life hinges on them — prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance (CCC 1834) — and prudence is described as the one that guides the rest: "Prudence is the virtue that disposes practical reason to discern our true good in every circumstance and to choose the right means of achieving it", called auriga virtutum, the charioteer of the virtues, because it "guides the other virtues by setting rule and measure" (CCC 1806). Aquinas supplies the technical scaffolding. Virtue is a habit — "human virtue is a habit" is the title of the first article of ST I–II q.55 — and more precisely an operative good habit; virtue is not in us by nature but is caused in us by habituation, and some moral virtues are also infused (ST I–II q.63 a.1–3). The infused virtues matter because the Catechism insists on them: the theological virtues of faith, hope and charity are "infused by God into the souls of the faithful" and "inform and give life to all the moral virtues" (CCC 1813), and CCC 1810 states the two-sided picture in one sentence: "Human virtues acquired by education, by deliberate acts and by a perseverance ever-renewed in repeated efforts are purified and elevated by divine grace." The tradition is also unsentimental about the difficulty: "It is not easy for man, wounded by sin, to maintain moral balance" (CCC 1811), which is why the virtues are matters of repeated practice and of grace rather than of resolve. Now the mechanism that makes this more than a vocabulary lesson. Because prudence is a virtue of practical reason that "takes cognizance of singulars" — the particulars of this situation — and because the moral virtues dispose the appetites so that reason can judge without being dragged, a person's habits determine not only what she does but what she notices and what appears to her as a reason for acting. The tradition states this as the claim that the virtuous person perceives differently: courage and cowardice do not merely produce different choices from an identical reading of the situation; they produce different readings. That is the sense in which character shapes moral vision, and it is why moral education in this tradition is a matter of formation rather than only of information. Two boundaries must be drawn around the claim, and both are contested in the contemporary literature. First, the empirical objection: the situationist critique associated with John Doris and Gilbert Harman argues, from experiments on helping behaviour and obedience, that conduct is driven more by situational features than by stable character traits, so that virtue ethics may overstate character's explanatory role. The honest answer is that these findings constrain what virtue claims can predict about behaviour under experimental pressure; they do not refute the claim that habituation changes a person's dispositions and practical judgement, and defenders note that virtue ethics is primarily a normative account of what a good person is and how she becomes one, not a predictor of scores in a laboratory. Second, a boundary inside Catholic moral theology itself: an account of virtue cannot replace the analysis of acts. Veritatis Splendor continues to insist that acts have a species from their object (VS 78–80, lesson 56), and the long-running renewal argument — the moral theologian Servais Pinckaers is its best-known proponent — is that a law-centred manual tradition had crowded out the older virtue-centred approach, not that the virtues make the norms unnecessary.
lessons.example: Work a case in which the same decision is available to two people with different habits, to see what the doctrine of virtue adds to the analysis of acts. Two accountants discover that a colleague has been misstating figures in a way that benefits the firm and that will be discovered within a year. Both see the same facts; both know that the act of reporting it is the honest one under lesson 56's analysis. Person A has for years practised small truthfulness, including in trivial matters where the cost was slight — habits formed by repeated deliberate acts (CCC 1804, 1810). Person B has for years taken the small convenient option, and has a settled habit of avoiding friction. Now run three claims the tradition makes and see how they appear in the case. Claim one, ease: what is arduous for B is relatively available to A, not because A has more willpower but because the habit has reorganised what she experiences as a live option — this is what CCC 1804 means by dispositions that make possible "ease, self-mastery, and joy". Claim two, perception: A notices the concrete human cost to the clients immediately; B's attention goes first to the personal risk. The tradition's claim that prudence "takes cognizance of singulars" (ST II–II q.47 a.3) explains why the difference shows up at the level of noticing rather than at the level of syllogism. Claim three, growth: the act itself is not neutral for either person — it is "the fruit and seed of morally good acts" (CCC 1804), so A's act strengthens a disposition and B's weakens one. That third claim is the reason the tradition treats virtue as a matter of direction of travel rather than of isolated transactions, and it is also what makes the pastoral language of gradual growth intelligible: a person's moral life has a trajectory, and the Church's pastoral documents describe accompaniment as patience with "the eventual stages of personal growth as these progressively appear" (Amoris Laetitia 308, which quotes Familiaris Consortio 9 and Gaudium et Spes 52). Now the second case, which shows the limits: a person of steady good habits encounters a genuinely novel situation — a medical decision with unfamiliar technology — and misjudges it badly. Nothing in virtue theory makes experience unnecessary; prudence depends on acquaintance with particulars, so a significant part of its acquisition is time, instruction and the counsel of those experienced in the domain. A learner who can explain both cases has understood why the tradition keeps virtue and analysis together: the analysis tells you what the right act is; the virtues make you the kind of person who can see and do it.
lessons.question: A retreat speaker tells a group that virtues are natural talents, so a person either has a generous disposition or does not, and no amount of practice will change it. Which correction reflects the tradition?
lessons.answer: Virtue is a habit rather than a natural endowment: it is not in us by nature but is caused in us by habituation, so it is acquired by repeated deliberate acts, is purified and elevated by grace, and can genuinely grow or decay (ST I–II q.63 a.1–2; CCC 1804, 1810).
lessons.distractor: The speaker is right in substance, since a person's temperament is fixed early and the virtues are simply the visible expression of that temperament.
lessons.correction: The tradition's anthropology is the opposite of the speaker's. Aquinas asks precisely whether virtue is in us by nature and answers no (ST I–II q.63 a.1), then asks whether any virtue is caused in us by habituation and answers yes (a.2), while also holding that some virtues are infused (a.3). The Catechism states the practical consequences: the moral virtues are acquired by human effort, grow 'through education, deliberate acts, and perseverance in struggle', and are purified and elevated by divine grace (CCC 1804, 1839, 1810). The correction matters pastorally as well as doctrinally: if virtues were fixed temperaments, moral formation and repentance would be pointless, and the Church's language about growth in holiness would be incoherent. Note what the correct claim does not say: it does not claim that habits are easy to change, or that temperament is irrelevant, or that a person can acquire practical wisdom without experience — CCC 1811 concedes that maintaining moral balance is not easy for a person wounded by sin.

depth.definitions: Virtue: an habitual and firm disposition to do good, permitting not only good acts but the giving of the best of oneself (CCC 1803); in Aquinas's terms an operative good habit of the soul (ST I–II q.55 a.1–3). Habit (habitus): a stable quality disposing a power to act in a certain way; the technical category that makes virtue a matter of formation rather than of momentary effort. Cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance — the hinges on which the moral life turns (CCC 1834). Prudence: the virtue of practical reason discerning the true good and the right means, called the charioteer of the virtues (CCC 1806; ST II–II q.47). Theological virtues: faith, hope and charity, infused by God, informing and giving life to the moral virtues (CCC 1813). Infused versus acquired virtue: virtues that God gives, distinct from those acquired by repeated acts, without which the moral life cannot reach its end (ST I–II q.63 a.3–4). Situationism: the empirical critique holding that behaviour is governed more by situational factors than by stable traits (Doris, Harman, among others). Moral vision: the claim that virtue shapes what a person perceives as salient and as a reason for acting, not merely the choice made after perception. Growth in virtue: the trajectory language of CCC 1810, 1839 and of pastoral documents such as Amoris Laetitia 308 on the stages of personal growth.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism of virtue is a feedback loop with three loops, and each can be stated plainly. Loop one, action to disposition: performing a good act makes the corresponding disposition more available, because the moral virtues are "the fruit and seed of morally good acts" (CCC 1804) — the seed image is doing real work, since it implies both that the act came from something and that it leaves something behind. Loop two, disposition to perception: a settled disposition alters what the practical reason sees, because prudence is concerned with singulars and the appetites can either support or distort practical judgement (ST I–II q.58 on the mutual dependence of moral and intellectual virtue; CCC 1806 on prudence setting rule and measure for the other virtues). Loop three, perception to act: what is noticed and what appears reasonable determine the choice, so the earlier loops shape decisions from the inside rather than in the manner of a constraint. Now the contested part of the mechanism, stated fairly. The situationist objection targets loop two, arguing that if character traits were robust, behaviour would show cross-situational consistency, and the experimental record shows more inconsistency than the trait account predicts. The Catholic reply has three moves worth knowing: that the experiments measure behaviour under unusual pressure rather than the ordinary functioning of character; that virtue theory's central claim is normative — what a flourishing person is and how character is formed — rather than predictive; and that the tradition's own analysis of prudence already concedes that judgement about singulars is difficult and can fail, which is why it insists on experience, counsel and grace (CCC 1811; ST I–II q.94 a.4 in the previous lesson). A learner who can state the objection without straw-manning it, and state the reply without pretending the objection is empty, is doing the intellectual work this lesson requires.
depth.secondExample: Take the same mechanism into a domain where the empirical literature is thick: medical practice. A clinician's habit of attention — the discipline of asking the second question, of not closing the diagnostic search on the first plausible answer — is a habit of the practical intellect, and its acquisition is not unlike the acquisition of prudence: it comes from education, deliberate practice and repeated effort (CCC 1810), and it is corrigible by experience. Note what is and is not being claimed. It is not claimed that the diligent clinician always reaches the right diagnosis; error remains possible and case series are full of misses. It is claimed that the habit changes what the clinician notices and how heavily she weighs what she notices, which is precisely why the training is worth doing. Now add the infused dimension, which is the part a purely secular virtue ethics cannot reproduce: the tradition holds that the theological virtues, infused by God, "inform and give life to all the moral virtues" (CCC 1813), so that the Christian's growth in virtue is not a self-improvement project but a participation in grace, and the moral life has a direction toward God rather than merely toward social competence. This explains a claim that otherwise looks strange: CCC 1828's contrast between the slave who avoids evil from fear of punishment, the mercenary who works for wages, and the son who acts for love of the good itself. The progression is not about different acts but about the person who acts, which is the whole point of a virtue-centred account.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. Error one, naturalising virtue: treating it as inborn temperament or talent, which contradicts ST I–II q.63 a.1 and makes moral formation meaningless. Error two, moralism by effort: treating virtue as willpower and forgetting that the tradition includes infused virtue and insists that the moral life is not sustainable by the wounded person alone (CCC 1811, 1813) — a mistake that turns the Gospel into a training programme. Error three, using virtue language as a substitute for analysis, so that "he is a good man" or "she meant well" is offered where the question was whether an act was right; this is the error that Veritatis Splendor 71–83 is written against, and lesson 56 gives the instrument to correct it, since the object of the act is not determined by the agent's general character. A fourth, subtler error is psychological determinism in the other direction: treating habits as so binding that a person cannot act against them, which contradicts the Church's teaching on freedom and responsibility and would make repentance unintelligible. Diagnostic: ask which of the three sources of morality (CCC 1750) a claim is actually about; if the claim is about the agent rather than the act, it belongs in this lesson, and if it is about the act, it belongs in lesson 56.
depth.application: Task: a virtue audit of one week, written up in about 500 words and kept private. (1) Choose two virtues from the cardinal set (CCC 1834) that you judge most relevant to your actual circumstances, and write one sentence each justifying the choice with a concrete situation. (2) For each virtue, identify one specific, small, repeatable act that would exercise it, and describe the minimum routine: how often, in what setting, and what would count as having done it. (3) Describe one situation from the past week in which your habits shaped what you noticed, stating what you noticed first and what you did not notice until later. (4) Name one virtue you lack and one circumstance in which that lack has produced a wrong act, keeping the description non-incriminating and general. (5) Ask one question of a pastor, spiritual director or trusted adviser about formation rather than about a decision. Self-review rubric: a strong audit has small and repeatable practices rather than grand resolutions; distinguishes what was done from what was noticed; does not collapse virtue into willpower, naming at least once where grace or help from others is needed; and contains no claim about being virtuous that the week's evidence does not support. A weak submission lists approved words, describes no concrete practice, or offers a decision-analysis instead of an audit of the person.
depth.summary: Virtue is a habit of the person, acquired through deliberate acts and capable of growth or decay, accompanied in the Christian life by infused virtues and ordered by prudence, which sets the measure for the others (CCC 1803–1806, 1810–1813, 1834; ST I–II q.55, q.63). The mechanism to carry away is the three-loop feedback of act, disposition and perception, together with the tradition's insistence that judgement about particulars is difficult and that the moral life is sustained by grace rather than by resolve. The empirical objection from situationism is a real constraint on what virtue theory can predict and does not dissolve the normative claim, so a serious learner can state it fairly and reply without pretending it is nothing. Keep the two boundaries from this lesson in place for the rest of the level: virtue formation is not a substitute for the analysis of acts (lesson 56), and prudential judgement in a concrete domain depends on experience and evidence, which is exactly what lesson 59 requires of medical cases and lesson 60 of a contested policy question where the analysis of acts and the formation of the decider are both in play.

lessons.title: Medical ethics at the beginning and end of life: where doctrine stops and judgement begins
lessons.explanation: Objective: know the defined prohibitions at each end of life, know the judgements the Church explicitly leaves open, and be able to tell them apart in a concrete case. At the beginning of life the Church's teaching rests on a claim about status that is stated without hedging: "Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception. From the first moment of his existence, a human being must be recognized as having the rights of a person" (CCC 2270), and "direct abortion, that is to say, abortion willed either as an end or a means, is gravely contrary to the moral law" (CCC 2271). Donum Vitae then applies that to reproductive technology by asking question-shaped headings, which makes it unusually easy to read: procreation must be the fruit of marriage and cannot be severed from the conjugal act, so heterologous artificial fertilization "is contrary to the unity of marriage, to the dignity of the spouses, to the vocation proper to parents, and to the child's right to be conceived and brought into the world in marriage and from marriage" (DV 2); surrogate motherhood is not licit "for the same reasons" (DV 3); and the conjugal act's unitive and procreative meanings may not be deliberately separated (DV 4). Dignitas Personae continues the analysis into newer techniques: embryo reduction "is an intentional selective abortion ... the deliberate and direct elimination of one or more innocent human beings in the initial phase of their existence" (DP 21); preimplantation diagnosis, because it is "immediately followed by the elimination of an embryo", shares the moral problem (DP 22); and the use of cell lines of illicit origin, including in vaccine production, is addressed with a notably differentiated judgement — there are "differing degrees of responsibility", and "grave reasons may be morally proportionate to justify the use of such 'biological material'. Thus, for example, danger to the health of children could permit parents to use a vaccine which was developed using cell lines of illicit origin, while keeping in mind that everyone has the duty to make known their disagreement and to ask that their healthcare system make other types of vaccines available" (DP 34). Read that sentence twice: it is a case where the Church's own document establishes a permission that many Catholics assume is forbidden, and it does so by an argument about cooperation and proportionality rather than by relaxing the prohibition on the original act. At the end of life the structure is similar but the prohibitions are more sharply defined. "Euthanasia in the strict sense is understood to be an action or omission which of itself and by intention causes death, with the purpose of eliminating all suffering", and the terms of reference "are to be found in the intention of the will and in the methods used" (Evangelium Vitae 65; the same definition opens section II of the 1980 Declaration on Euthanasia); direct euthanasia "is morally unacceptable" (CCC 2277). But the same paragraph of Evangelium Vitae immediately distinguishes the withholding of treatment: "Euthanasia must be distinguished from the decision to forego so-called 'aggressive medical treatment', in other words, medical procedures which no longer correspond to the real situation of the patient", and it adds that "to forego extraordinary or disproportionate means is not the equivalent of suicide or euthanasia; it rather expresses acceptance of the human condition in the face of death" (EV 65). The Catechism states the permission and its boundary: discontinuing procedures that are "burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary, or disproportionate" can be legitimate, and in such a case "one does not will to cause death; one's inability to impede it is merely accepted" (CCC 2278) — while "even if death is thought imminent, the ordinary care owed to a sick person cannot be legitimately interrupted", and painkillers that may shorten life are permissible "if death is not willed as either an end or a means, but only foreseen and tolerated as inevitable" (CCC 2279). On nutrition and hydration the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith answered the American bishops' questions in five responses, holding that administering food and water even artificially "is, in principle, an ordinary and proportionate means of preserving life" and "therefore obligatory to the extent to which, and for as long as, it is shown to accomplish its proper finality" (2007 responses, first and second questions). Samaritanus Bonus (2020) gathers the discipline into one document whose section headings map the terrain: the prohibition of euthanasia and assisted suicide; "the moral obligation to exclude aggressive medical treatment"; basic care and the requirement of nutrition and hydration; palliative care; the role of the family and hospice; analgesic therapy and loss of consciousness; and pastoral accompaniment. Two further judgements should be noted because they show the Church refusing to claim competence she does not have. On the determination of death, John Paul II told transplant specialists that "the Church does not make technical decisions" about the criteria used to ascertain death, and that the neurological criterion of "the complete and irreversible cessation of all brain activity, if rigorously applied, does not seem to conflict with the essential elements of a sound anthropology" (Address to the Transplantation Society, 29 August 2000) — a technical judgement the Church declines to make, offered with the caveat of moral certainty rather than certainty. And organ donation after death "is a noble and meritorious act and is to be encouraged as a manifestation of generous solidarity", provided consent is explicit (CCC 2296). What follows is where the live arguments are, and they are worth naming as arguments rather than resolving. First, the determination of death: because the Church declines the technical decision, Catholic scholars continue to debate whether neurological criteria identify death, and this is a dispute about medicine and anthropology rather than about a defined teaching. Second, what counts as proportionate: the 2007 responses were themselves produced by a dispute among moralists and bishops about patients in a vegetative state, and the answer they give — obligatoriness conditioned by whether the means accomplishes its purpose and by excessive burden — leaves judgements that reasonable Catholics make differently about particular patients. Third, whether stopping eating and drinking voluntarily is a refusal of treatment or an act with the intention of ending life: Catholic moralists divide, and the Church has not settled it. Fourth, the distribution of scarce resources and the justice of health-care systems, where the Church's social teaching constrains the answer but does not supply it.
lessons.example: Work one end-of-life case through the instruments, answering five questions and labelling the status of each answer. The case: an elderly woman with advanced cancer, competent and clear, whose pain is poorly controlled, whose family asks whether "everything" should be done, and whose doctors propose a transfer to intensive care if her breathing deteriorates. Question one: may she refuse chemotherapy or the transfer to intensive care? Yes — this is the refusal of disproportionate or burdensome means, explicitly distinguished from euthanasia (EV 65) and permitted at CCC 2278, with the decisions to be made by the patient if competent. Question two: may she, or anyone, arrange a lethal injection if suffering becomes unbearable? No — this is direct euthanasia, an act which "of itself and by intention causes death, with the purpose of eliminating all suffering", and the Catechism calls it "morally unacceptable" whatever the motives or means (CCC 2277; EV 65). This prohibition is defined teaching, not a prudential judgement, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than softening it. Question three: may she receive opioid analgesia in doses that may suppress respiration? Yes, if the death is not willed as end or means but only foreseen and tolerated (CCC 2279) — and the analysis here is the double-effect structure of lesson 56, applied to a case the Catechism itself supplies. Question four: may hydration and nutrition be stopped? Not as a general policy, because the 2007 responses hold artificial administration to be in principle ordinary and proportionate and therefore obligatory so long as it accomplishes its purpose and is not excessively burdensome; but whether it is accomplishing its purpose in this patient, and whether it is disproportionately burdensome, are judgements about particulars that require medical assessment and carry no defined answer in advance — which is exactly where the argument among moralists lives. Question five: may her organs be donated, and when is death established? Donation is encouraged if consent is explicit (CCC 2296), and the determination of death is a technical determination about which the Church declines to legislate (Address, 2000), so the moral obligation here is that the criteria be rigorously applied rather than that any particular criterion be adopted. Now notice what the exercise has produced: one defined prohibition (direct killing), one defined permission (refusing disproportionate means), one defined permission with conditions (analgesia under double effect), one obligation with a judgement about its scope (nutrition and hydration), and one matter explicitly delegated to medicine (the determination of death). A learner who reports all five as "the Church says no" or all five as "the Church says it is up to you" has lost the distinctions the lesson exists to teach, and a parish or family that loses them will either prolong dying by aggressive means or approve of killing, both of which the same documents forbid.
lessons.question: A family asks a priest whether stopping a ventilator for a patient with no hope of recovery is euthanasia. Which answer best reflects the Church's teaching?
lessons.answer: It depends on the act and intention: withdrawing treatment that is disproportionate or burdensome is permitted, because one does not will the death but merely accepts the inability to impede it (CCC 2278), whereas an action or omission that of itself and by intention causes death in order to eliminate suffering is euthanasia and is never permitted (CCC 2277; EV 65).
lessons.distractor: It is euthanasia in every case, because any action or omission that results in the patient's death, including removing a ventilator, is morally equivalent to killing, and the Church forbids it without exception.
lessons.correction: The family's question is genuine because the two cases look identical at the level of outcome and differ at the level of act and intention. The Church distinguishes them explicitly: withholding or withdrawing procedures that "no longer correspond to the real situation of the patient" is not euthanasia but "acceptance of the human condition in the face of death" (EV 65), and CCC 2278 says that in discontinuing burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary or disproportionate procedures "one does not will to cause death; one's inability to impede it is merely accepted". Direct euthanasia, by contrast, is defined as an action or omission which of itself and by intention causes death in order to end suffering (EV 65; CCC 2277) and is defined teaching against which no motive or circumstance can be weighed. The distinction is not a loophole: it fails if death itself is the means chosen to secure a benefit, and it also fails if ordinary care — nutrition, hydration, warmth, pain relief, presence — is interrupted simply because death is imminent (CCC 2279). So the correct answer to the family is a procedure, not a verdict: establish what the treatment is accomplishing, what the patient wants, and what is being chosen.

depth.definitions: Direct abortion: abortion willed either as an end or as a means, gravely contrary to the moral law and taught as such without exception (CCC 2271). Direct euthanasia: an act or omission which of itself and by intention causes death in order to eliminate all suffering (EV 65; Declaration on Euthanasia II; CCC 2277). Aggressive or disproportionate treatment: medical procedures that no longer correspond to the patient's real situation because the burdens outweigh the expected benefit; forgoing them is not euthanasia (EV 65; CCC 2278). Ordinary care: basic care owed to every patient, which cannot be interrupted even when death is thought imminent (CCC 2279). Double effect: the analysis permitting an act with a foreseen but unintended harmful effect when the harm is not the means to the good and the act is proportionate (lesson 56; applied to analgesia at CCC 2279). Illicit-origin biological material: cell lines derived from an act against human life or integrity, whose use is analysed by cooperation and proportionality, with "grave reasons" capable of justifying use in some cases (DP 34). Determination of death: the technical ascertainment of death, which the Church declines to make, while noting that the neurological criterion rigorously applied "does not seem to conflict with the essential elements of a sound anthropology" (Address to the Transplantation Society, 2000). Conscientious objection: the refusal of direct cooperation with euthanasia or abortion, explicitly invoked in Evangelium Vitae 89 and developed in Samaritanus Bonus. Pastoral accompaniment: the Church's insistence that the dying must not be abandoned, formalised in Samaritanus Bonus's section on accompaniment and the sacraments.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that keeps these cases coherent is a two-part question, and both parts must be answered before any verdict. Part one: what is the object of the act, described as the proximate end of the one choosing (VS 78, lesson 56)? If the object is "the death of this person, chosen to end suffering", the analysis ends at a defined prohibition, and no consideration of proportion changes it (CCC 2277). If the object is "the relief of pain", "the withdrawal of a treatment that burdens without benefit", or "the provision of food and water", the analysis continues. Part two: what are the circumstances and burdens, and what is the intention? Here the Church states objective conditions — whether a means "is shown to accomplish its proper finality" and whether it causes significant physical discomfort or is excessively burdensome (2007 responses) — and then leaves the application to clinical judgement and conscience, which is why two faithful Catholics can differ about a particular patient's nutrition and hydration without either denying the teaching. Note the structural role of the second part: it is not a discretionary escape hatch but the ordinary operation of prudence, and it is why the documents speak about facts ("shown to accomplish its proper finality") rather than issuing rules. Finally, note what the mechanism forbids in the other direction: it does not permit a bishop, a chaplain or a family to convert the refusal of disproportionate means into a licence for intending death, and it does not permit physicians to treat a prognosis of shortened life as authorising the withdrawal of ordinary care, which CCC 2279 expressly protects. Both abuses are documented, and the documents restrain both.
depth.secondExample: Take a contrasting case from the beginning of life so that the same mechanism is visible across the whole field: a couple using in-vitro fertilisation in which several embryos will be created, some transferred and some frozen or discarded, and the clinic offering preimplantation genetic testing to select for a child free of a heritable condition. Prohibitions first: the deliberate destruction of embryos is the elimination of innocent human beings and is excluded (DP 21, 22); selecting embryos against a disabling condition carries the additional problem of treating the child as a product to specification, and DP 22 notes that the diagnosis is "immediately followed by the elimination" of the embryos not transferred, which is the feature that makes the practice inseparable from killing in ordinary use. Now the part that surprises learners: the same documents contain permissions. Parents may use a vaccine developed from an illicit-origin cell line for grave reasons, including danger to their children's health, while registering their disagreement and pressing for alternatives (DP 34), and this is an application of the very cooperation analysis that classical moral theology developed for cases of material cooperation with another's wrong. The structural lesson is identical at both ends of life: the Church defines a small set of acts as always excluded, and then reasons carefully about the world in which people must act, permitting what is not excluded — sometimes with a permission that contradicts the stereotype of the Church held by her friends as well as by her critics. A learner who can name one such permission and one such prohibition, each with a citation, has understood that the teaching is a reasoned structure rather than a list of anxieties.
depth.mistake: Four mistakes recur. Mistake one, collapsing the end-of-life distinctions: treating any withdrawal of treatment that shortens life as euthanasia, which contradicts EV 65 and CCC 2278 and would oblige families to continue burdensome treatment that the Church says they may decline. Mistake two, widening the permission: treating "proportionate" as "whatever the patient or the family prefers", which converts a judgement governed by objective conditions into a preference, and which CCC 2279 rules out by protecting ordinary care even when death is imminent. Mistake three, missing the beginning-of-life prohibitions: treating embryo destruction as a technical detail so long as the resulting pregnancy is wanted, which DP 21 and 22 address directly. Mistake four, overgeneralising the cooperation permission: reading DP 34's "grave reasons" as a general licence to cooperate with illicit-origin research, when the document requires differentiating degrees of responsibility, the absence of alternatives where possible, and the duty "to make known their disagreement". A practical diagnostic: ask the learner to write two lists headed ALWAYS EXCLUDED and LEFT TO JUDGEMENT and then to place five propositions. The most common single failure is putting the withdrawal of burdensome treatment on the excluded list, or putting the determination of death there, when the Church treats the second as technical and the first as permitted.
depth.application: Task: prepare a one-page briefing for a hypothetical ethics committee, on a case you construct with no real patients and no identifying details, involving either a beginning-of-life or an end-of-life decision. Required components: (1) THE FACTS: five lines of clinical and social facts, including what the patient or parties want; (2) ACT AND INTENTION: two sentences, one naming the proximate end of the proposed decision, one naming what is not intended, worded so that the double-effect structure of lesson 56 could be applied; (3) THE PROHIBITIONS: identify any defined prohibition implicated, with a citation, and state plainly whether it applies or not; (4) THE JUDGEMENTS: identify the judgements the Church leaves open — proportionality, burden, the purpose a treatment is serving — and say who is competent to make each one; (5) THE QUESTIONS THE CHURCH DECLINES: state which part of the case is technical or prudential and explicitly not the Church's to determine; (6) UNSETTLED: name one point on which Catholic moralists themselves disagree, and say that it is disputed rather than settled. Self-review rubric: full credit requires at least four correct citations with paragraph numbers, a clear separation between prohibitions and judgements, and a correct identification of a point of genuine disagreement among Catholics. A briefing that resolves everything as either forbidden or permitted, or that invents a magisterial rule where the Church has expressed none, fails: the standing limitation of this lesson is that written exercises can test whether you can run the analysis, not whether you possess the prudence the analysis requires.
depth.summary: The structure of Catholic medical ethics at both ends of life is a small set of defined prohibitions surrounded by a large field of reasoned judgement. Defined: direct abortion (CCC 2271), the deliberate destruction of embryos (DP 21–22), surrogate motherhood and heterologous fertilisation (DV 2–3), and direct euthanasia (CCC 2277; EV 65). Judgement: whether a treatment is proportionate or burdensome (CCC 2278; EV 65), what a means of nutrition and hydration is accomplishing in this patient (2007 responses), whether analgesia's foreseen effect on life is intended (CCC 2279), and what counts as ordinary care that may never be interrupted. Delegated: the determination of death, which the Church explicitly declines to decide technically (Address, 2000), and the distribution of scarce resources. Permitted in ways that surprise: the withdrawal of disproportionate treatment, organ donation, analgesia with foreseen risk, and — under "grave reasons" — the use of a vaccine developed from an illicit-origin cell line, with the duty to register disagreement and seek alternatives (DP 34). Carry this structure into the capstone, which requires exactly the same discipline: to state the doctrinal constraints, to identify the judgements the Church leaves to prudence and evidence, and to be honest about which disagreements are not doctrinal at all.

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Donum Vitae (1987), introduction and part I
readings.note: The document is organised as numbered questions and answers, which makes it unusually easy to read selectively: the requirement that procreation be the fruit of marriage (1), heterologous fertilisation (2), surrogate motherhood (3), the inseparability of the unitive and procreative meanings (4), homologous IVF (5) and homologous insemination (6), the criterion for medical intervention (7) and the suffering caused by infertility (8).

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Dignitas Personae (2008), 4, 21–22 and 34
readings.note: Read 4 for the framing, 21 for embryo reduction, 22 for preimplantation diagnosis, and 34 for the illicit-origin biological material question including the vaccine example and the duty to register disagreement. Paragraph 34 is the single most instructive passage for understanding how the Church reasons about cooperation.

readings.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, respect for human life (CCC 2270–2279) and transplants (CCC 2296)
readings.note: 2270–2275 for the beginning of life, 2276–2279 for the dying — with 2278 on discontinuing disproportionate treatment and 2279 on ordinary care and analgesia — and 2296 for organ donation. Locate each paragraph by number in the index.

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Declaration on Euthanasia (Iura et Bona, 1980), sections II–IV
readings.note: Section II defines euthanasia and states the prohibition; III addresses the means available and the distinction between ordinary and extraordinary means; IV addresses the use of painkillers even at the risk of shortening life. This is the source of the formulations the Catechism and Evangelium Vitae later reuse.

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Samaritanus Bonus (2020), sections I–V
readings.note: The consolidated treatment. Read the table of contents for the structure and then the section on the moral obligation to exclude aggressive medical treatment, the section on basic care and nutrition and hydration, and the sections on palliative care and on accompaniment, including its warnings about end-of-life protocols such as Do Not Resuscitate orders and its treatment of conscientious objection.

readings.title: John Paul II, Address to the participants in the Transplantation Congress (29 August 2000)
readings.note: The clearest example in the whole corpus of the Church limiting her own competence: on the criteria used to ascertain death she says the Church does not make technical decisions, and offers the assessment that the neurological criterion rigorously applied does not seem to conflict with a sound anthropology. Read it for both halves — the technical deference and the moral conditions attached to it.

visual.title: Two-part analysis for medical decisions at the edges of life
visual.description: A flowchart that forces the object of the act to be identified before any consideration of outcome, then routes the case into a defined prohibition, a permitted act, or a judgement left to prudence and medicine.
steps: Entry: state the case as a proposed act or omission and write one sentence naming the proximate end of the choice (VS 78; CCC 1751).

Gate A, DEFINED PROHIBITION: does the choice intend the death or the destruction of an innocent person, whether as end or as means? If yes, stop — direct abortion (CCC 2271), deliberate embryo destruction (DP 21–22), direct euthanasia (CCC 2277; EV 65).

If no, Gate B, PERMITTED IN PRINCIPLE: is the choice the withholding or withdrawal of treatment that is burdensome or disproportionate? Then it is permitted, and one 'does not will to cause death' (CCC 2278; EV 65).

Lane C, PERMITTED WITH CONDITIONS: analgesia whose foreseen effect may shorten life, licit only if death is not willed as end or means (CCC 2279); organ donation, encouraged with explicit consent (CCC 2296).

Lane D, JUDGEMENT LEFT OPEN: whether a particular treatment is proportionate, whether nutrition and hydration in this patient accomplish their proper finality (2007 responses), and what 'ordinary care' requires in the circumstances.

Terminal box, DELEGATED TO MEDICINE: the determination of death — 'the Church does not make technical decisions' (Address, 2000) — with a note that ordinary care may never be interrupted even when death is imminent (CCC 2279).

lessons.title: Capstone: weighing a contested prudential judgement, using migration policy as the case
lessons.explanation: Objective: run the whole level's method on a contested policy question, and produce an answer that is both substantively positioned and honest about what the Church settles and what she leaves to argument. The method has six steps, and the case is migration. Step one, state the question precisely. "Is the Church for open borders?" is not one question. The questions actually on the table are: what does the Church teach that constrains any migration policy; which proposed measures are compatible with that teaching; what would the measures in fact do; and who decides. Step two, sort the claims — doctrinal, empirical, prudential, and ecclesial-institutional — as lesson 55 did for environmental questions. Step three, apply the analysis of acts: what is chosen, with what intention, and with what circumstances (lesson 56), because some policy instruments have objects that cannot be rescued by good consequences. Step four, ask who is competent, and be specific, since the Church's own documents divide the question. Step five, ask what would change your mind, which is the discipline that separates an argument from a slogan. Step six, name what you would not settle from where you sit. Now the doctrine, which is more two-sided than either party to the public argument usually admits. The Catechism states both obligations in a single paragraph: "The more prosperous nations are obliged, to the extent they are able, to welcome the foreigner in search of the security and the means of livelihood which he cannot find in his country of origin", and "public authorities should see to it that the natural right is respected that places a guest under the protection of those who receive him" — then, in the same paragraph, "political authorities, for the sake of the common good for which they are responsible, may make the exercise of the right to immigrate subject to various juridical conditions", while immigrants "are obliged to respect with gratitude the material and spiritual heritage of the country that receives them, to obey its laws and to assist in carrying civic burdens" (CCC 2241). The same pair appears in the Holy See's instruction on migration, which records that the Council "reaffirmed the right to emigrate" and "recognised the right of the public authorities, in a particular context, to regulate the flow of migration" (Erga Migrantes Caritas Christi 21, citing Gaudium et Spes 65 and 87), and it names the state's legitimate interest in an immigration policy that "promotes the common good" while also affirming repeated magisterial insistence on "the fundamental rights of the person, in particular the right to emigrate", the right not to be forced to emigrate, family unity and the protection of minors, together with the rejection of "all sentiments and manifestations of xenophobia and racism" and of "every possible discrimination" (EMCC 30, 21). Fratelli Tutti presses the moral demand hard without withdrawing the state's competence: it describes the fear of migrants as "part of our natural instinct of self-defence" (FT 41), and simultaneously insists that "the limits and borders of individual states cannot stand in the way" of the claim that no one should be excluded by place of birth (FT 121) and that "each country also belongs to the foreigner, inasmuch as a territory's goods must not be denied to a needy person coming from elsewhere" (FT 124). And the social teaching's structural principle applies throughout: the priority of the poor and the demand that goods reach those who need them (CCC 2444, and the intergenerational and universal common good of CCC 1905–1912). Note that no magisterial document determines a quota, a visa category, a wall, a fleet, an enforcement budget or a development-aid formula; and note also that no magisterial document leaves the question unconstrained. Some positions really are excluded: a policy whose object is the deliberate humiliation, collective punishment or exposure to death of persons as such has an object that cannot be willed; a policy that treats persons made in God's image as mere instruments of deterrence fails the priority of labour over capital's underlying principle, that persons are never merely means; and a policy that denies the rights that the Catechism says "precede any society", or that requires citizens to act against the fundamental rights of persons (CCC 2242), cannot be justified by its good effects. Everything else — levels, sequencing, reciprocity, enforcement mechanisms, the balance between border control and legal pathways, the weight of fiscal and labour-market considerations, the prudential judgement about whether a given message deters smuggling or fuels it — is argued, and faithful Catholics argue it in opposite directions. That is not a defect in the teaching; it is what the teaching's own structure predicts, and the last sentence of this explanation is the thesis of the whole level: the Church tells you what you may not do and why, and then leaves you the work of deciding what you should do.
lessons.example: Take a concrete legislative package and analyse it, not to reach a verdict but to show what a careful Catholic argument looks like on any side. The package contains four provisions: (A) increased border enforcement, including more physical barriers and a larger detention capacity; (B) a legalisation pathway for long-resident undocumented workers meeting work and tax conditions; (C) a binding requirement that children be separated from parents only in exceptional, judicially reviewed circumstances, with family reunification mandated; (D) increased development assistance to principal sending countries. Run the six steps on each. Step one, the question for each provision is a different question: A asks what enforcement is proportionate and effective; B asks whether legal status should be granted and on what conditions; C asks whether a practice violates fundamental rights; D asks whether aid reduces or displaces migration. Step two, sorting: the obligation to welcome, the right to regulate for the common good, the rejection of discrimination and xenophobia, the protection of the family and of minors, and the priority of the poor are doctrinal (CCC 2241, 2444; EMCC 21, 30); the effects of walls, detention and aid on migration flows are empirical and heavily contested by economists who disagree in good faith; and the level of enforcement spending relative to legalisation processing is prudential. Step three, act analysis: provision C is where moral analysis, rather than empirical dispute, is decisive, because if separation is chosen as a means of deterrence then the child's suffering is the instrument, and an act whose object is the harm of an innocent person cannot be rescued by the good it secures — this is lesson 56's structure, not an intuition. Provision A may be defended or attacked; the moral question is what specific acts it involves (detention conditions, denial of hearings, treatment of asylum claimants) rather than the fact of enforcement. Provision B engages the goods of work, family and social participation, and its conditions must be tested for arbitrariness and for the exclusion of the vulnerable. Provision D engages the duty of the rich nations toward the poor, with the honest caveat that whether aid reduces pressure is an empirical claim, not a moral one. Step four, competence: the Church teaches the norms (bishops, the Catechism, the Holy See's instruction); economists and migration scholars assess the empirical claims; the political community decides the prudential balance; and a parish council decides none of them. Step five, what would change your mind: evidence that a given enforcement measure had no deterrent effect and large humanitarian costs would remove one side's argument for it; evidence that a legalisation pathway produced exploitation or fraud would do the same on the other side. Step six, what is not yours to settle: a parish, whatever it thinks, may not treat a prudential disagreement about enforcement levels as a test of orthodoxy, and it may not pretend that the Church's teaching commits her to one of the competing policy packages. The two Catholic positions that emerge from this analysis are both serious: one emphasises the duty of welcome, the rights that precede society, and the moral weight of the excluded poor; the other emphasises the state's responsibility for the common good, the need for law's integrity, and the claim that a disordered system harms the poor it claims to help. Both cite the magisterium. Neither is dissent.
lessons.question: A parish discussion collapses into two claims: one person says the Church's teaching requires a policy of open borders, and another says the Church has no teaching on immigration because it is a purely political matter. Which assessment is accurate?
lessons.answer: Both are wrong: the Church does teach binding norms on migration — the duty of prosperous nations to welcome, the rights that precede society, family unity, the rejection of discrimination (CCC 2241; EMCC 21, 30; FT 121, 124) — while explicitly recognising the public authority's right to regulate the flow of migration for the common good, so the teaching constrains policy without prescribing one.
lessons.distractor: The first claim is correct: since the Church teaches that each country belongs to the foreigner and borders cannot stand in the way, any restriction on immigration is contrary to Church teaching.
lessons.correction: The first claim quotes real texts out of a structure that also contains their counterparts. Fratelli Tutti 121 and 124 do insist that place of birth must not exclude anyone and that each country belongs to the foreigner; but the Catechism in the same paragraph that imposes the duty of welcome adds that political authorities "may make the exercise of the right to immigrate subject to various juridical conditions" for the sake of the common good (CCC 2241), and the Holy See's migration instruction records that the Council reaffirmed the right to emigrate and simultaneously "recognised the right of the public authorities, in a particular context, to regulate the flow of migration" (EMCC 21). The second claim, that there is no teaching at all, is equally false and for the same reason: the documents are full of norms that exclude real policies, including those whose object is to harm persons as a means of deterrence. The accurate position is the harder one: the teaching is binding, and it does not entail a single policy package. That means a participant in the discussion who accuses the other of bad faith either because they defend a legalisation pathway or because they defend enforcement has substituted a test of orthodoxy for an argument about prudence.

depth.definitions: Prudential judgement: judgement about the means to be chosen in contingent circumstances, which the Church does not make for the political community; its classical home is the virtue of prudence (CCC 1806; lesson 58). Right to emigrate: the right affirmed by the Council and repeated by the Holy See's migration instruction, together with the right not to be forced to emigrate and the right to remain in one's own country. Common good: the sum of social conditions allowing people to reach fulfilment more fully and more easily (CCC 1906), including the universal common good of the human family (CCC 1911). Universal destination of goods: the principle that created goods are destined for all, which underlies the claim that a territory's goods must not be denied to a needy person from elsewhere (FT 124). Fundamental rights that precede society: rights grounded in the dignity of the person as created by God rather than granted by the state (FT 124; CCC 2273 on the same logic). Object of an act: the proximate end chosen, which determines whether an act can be willed at all (VS 78; CCC 1751). Excluded policy: a policy whose act-description is intrinsically disordered, for example one that instruments the suffering of innocent persons as a means of deterrence. Competence: the principle that different questions belong to different authorities, decisive here because doctrine, empirical assessment and prudential choice are held by different people. Sensus fidei and the obedience owed to non-definitive teaching: the mode of assent that governs how a Catholic should weigh bishops' judgements on political matters (lesson 46).
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that keeps a contested policy argument from becoming a shouting match has four gears, and each has a failure mode. Gear one, separating kinds of claim: doctrinal norms, empirical predictions and prudential choices are asserted with different kinds of warrant, and the commonest manoeuvre in a bad argument is to assert an empirical claim with the certainty of a norm ("enforcement always deters") or to assert a norm with the tentativeness of a prediction ("welcoming migrants is one option among others"). Gear two, applying the analysis of acts before the analysis of consequences: if a measure's object involves instrumenting the harm of persons, the consequences are irrelevant to its permissibility, not merely outweighed by them (lesson 56; CCC 1754). Gear three, distributing competence: the Church teaches, the scholar estimates, the legislator decides, and the pastor accompanies — and much of the heat in parish arguments comes from people exercising a competence that is not theirs, in either direction, since a pastor who announces a legislative preference from the pulpit and a parishioner who announces that the Church has nothing to say are making the same error from opposite ends. Gear four, stating what would change your mind: a position that cannot name any evidence that would alter it has left the domain of prudential argument, which is what the Church means when she says these questions are not hers to settle but belong to the virtue of prudence exercised by citizens. Putting the four gears together produces the characteristic output of this level: a judgement that is real, argued, fallible and owed to others, rather than either a slogan or an abstention.
depth.secondExample: Run the same four gears on a second contested case to prove the method transfers: whether a Catholic legislator may vote for a budget that funds services she regards as gravely wrong, in order to secure provisions she regards as gravely important. Gear one sorts the claims: what the Church defines about the wrong in question; what the empirical consequences of voting against the budget would actually be; what the legislator's own responsibility is for another's wrong act. Gear two asks what she is choosing: if her object is to limit a serious harm while accepting a cooperator's act she does not will, the classical analysis distinguishes immediate from mediate material cooperation and asks about proportionality and scandal; if her object is to secure the wrong act as a means, the analysis stops. Gear three identifies competence: the moral theologian analyses cooperation, the legislator judges the legislative arithmetic, and the bishop may counsel — but no one can substitute for the legislator's own formed conscience, which is why lesson 46 (formed conscience and dissent) and lesson 39 precede this lesson in the course. Gear four demands that she state what evidence would change her vote. The point of the pair of cases — migration and legislative cooperation — is that the capstone is not about migration at all: it is about the ability to hold a genuinely contested question without either collapsing it into a slogan or fleeing into abstention, which is the intellectual habit this level has been building since lesson 51.
depth.mistake: Four errors, all common in real discussion. Error one, single-policy maximalism: asserting that the Church's teaching entails one policy package — open borders, on one reading, or the strictest enforcement, on the other — which the documents refute in the same paragraphs that state the duty of welcome and the state's competence (CCC 2241; EMCC 21). Error two, total abstention: treating the question as purely political and therefore morally weightless, which abandons the people the norms protect and misreads Fratelli Tutti's insistence that no one should be excluded by place of birth (FT 121, 124). Error three, consequence-only reasoning: defending a measure by its aggregate benefits when the measure's object involves harming persons as a means, which is precisely the error lesson 56 exists to catch (CCC 1754; VS 80). Error four, moralising the empirical: treating contested findings about deterrence or labour-market effects as though they were settled by the Church's authority, in whichever direction suits one's prior preference. Diagnostic for any contribution to the argument: ask the speaker to state (a) the norm they think applies, with a citation; (b) the empirical claim on which their policy preference rests; (c) the evidence that would change their mind; and (d) the authority they think should decide. A contribution that cannot answer all four is an opinion, which is legitimate to hold but not to impose as Church teaching.
depth.application: Task: the level's capstone paper, of about 1,200 words, on a contested prudential question of your choosing — migration policy is the worked case, but a policy question in health care allocation, penal policy, education funding or climate policy is equally acceptable. The paper must contain, with clear headings: (1) THE QUESTION, stated as a decision someone could actually make, not as a slogan; (2) THE NORMS, with at least three citations from magisterial documents, each quoted in not more than fifteen words and correctly attributed, plus one sentence for each stating what it constrains; (3) THE ACT ANALYSIS, applying object, intention and circumstance to the specific measure at issue, and naming any part of the measure whose object is excluded; (4) THE EMPIRICAL CLAIMS, two predictions on which your preference depends, with a note on the evidence that would confirm or refute each; (5) THE PRUDENTIAL JUDGEMENT, your position, with the strongest opposing Catholic position stated in a form its advocate would accept, and your reason for preferring yours; (6) WHAT YOU WOULD NOT SETTLE, naming at least one thing you decline to resolve and who holds competence for it; (7) THE LIMIT OF THIS EXERCISE, one honest sentence stating that a written analysis and a retrieval quiz cannot certify prudence, and that the Church's own teaching requires a formed conscience rather than a correct answer sheet. Self-review rubric: full credit requires that every quotation is verifiable in the source; that norms are distinguished from predictions and from preferences; that at least one part of the analysis shows the act analysis doing decisive work rather than the consequences; that the opposing position is not a caricature; and that section seven is present and specific. A paper that reaches a conclusion by aggregation of harms, or that treats disagreement as bad faith, fails regardless of its political direction.
depth.summary: The level closes with an instrument rather than an answer: sort claims by kind, analyse the act before the consequences, distribute competence, and state what would change your mind. Applied to migration, it yields a two-sided result that is easy to state and hard to practise — binding norms that exclude some policies, notably those that instrument the harm of persons, and a prudential question that the Church does not answer for the political community, which is why faithful Catholics argue the same texts in opposing directions (CCC 2241; EMCC 21, 30; FT 41, 121, 124). The same instrument has been the working method of every lesson in this level: work and vocation distinguished doctrine from policy (lesson 51), marriage distinguished the bond from its pastoral application (lesson 52), the theology of the body distinguished catechesis from definition (lesson 53), the states of life distinguished doctrine from discipline (lesson 54), creation care distinguished the moral frame from the empirical judgement (lesson 55), moral method supplied the analysis of acts (lesson 56), natural law supplied the structure of the norms (lesson 57), virtue explained how a person becomes able to judge (lesson 58), and medical ethics showed a defined prohibition standing beside judgements the Church explicitly delegates (lesson 59). If you can carry that sorting habit into an argument you care about, in church or in public, this level has done its work. What it has not done, and cannot do, is certify that you will judge well: that is the work of prudence, experience, counsel and grace (CCC 1806, 1810–1811).

readings.title: Pontifical Council for the Pastoral Care of Migrants and Itinerant People, Erga Migrantes Caritas Christi (2004), Part I and 21, 30
readings.note: The Holy See's systematic instruction. Read 21 for the Council's two-sided legacy — the right to emigrate and the public authority's right to regulate the flow of migration — and 30 for the rights of migrants, family unity, the protection of minors and the rejection of discrimination and xenophobia. Part I also treats migration as a sign of the times and Mt 25:35 as its scriptural anchor.

readings.title: Francis, Fratelli Tutti (2020), 37–41 and 121–125
readings.note: 37–41 for the section on migrants and the borders, including the acknowledgement in 41 that hesitancy and fear are part of a natural instinct of self-defence; 121 for the claim that no one may be excluded because of place of birth, and 124 for the application of the universal destination of goods to territories. Read both parts: the moral demand and the admitted fear are in the same document.

readings.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church: immigrants, the duties of citizens and the common good (CCC 2241–2242 and 1905–1912)
readings.note: CCC 2241 is the key paragraph and should be read whole: the duty of prosperous nations to welcome, the protection owed to the guest, the authorities' power to attach juridical conditions to immigration for the common good, and the immigrants' duties. CCC 2242 supplies the limits of obedience to civil authority, and 1905–1912 the account of the common good. Locate paragraphs by number in the index.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes, 65–66 and 87
readings.note: 65–66 for development, inequality and the duty of nations — the texts the Holy See cites when it states the right to emigrate — and 87 for the conciliar basis of the public authority's competence over migration. Read 43 and 76 as well if you want the conciliar account of the laity's competence in temporal affairs, which is the doctrinal warrant for saying the policy question is not the Church's to decide.

readings.title: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, Migration Committee: Catholic social teaching on immigration
readings.note: One national bishops' conference's statement of the teaching and of its own policy positions, useful as a worked example of a bishops' conference drawing prudential conclusions that other Catholics dispute. Caveat for the publisher and the learner: USCCB pages frequently refuse automated clients with a 403 while rendering normally in a browser, so if a script cannot read the page, open it directly.

visual.title: Capstone template: six steps for a contested prudential judgement
visual.description: A vertical flow that takes a contested policy question and routes it through question-stating, sorting, act analysis, competence, falsifiability and non-settlement, with the migration case annotated at each step.
steps: Step 1, STATE THE QUESTION as a decision: 'should the legislature attach conditions X and Y to legal status?' — not 'is the Church for open borders?'.

Step 2, SORT THE CLAIMS into four columns: doctrinal norms (cited), empirical predictions (evidence-dependent), prudential choices (argued), and ecclesial-institutional positions (a bishops' conference's own judgement).

Step 3, ANALYSE THE ACT: name the proximate end of the measure (VS 78), and mark any part whose object is excluded — for example a measure that instruments the suffering of children as a means of deterrence (CCC 1754).
Step 4, DISTRIBUTE COMPETENCE: the Church teaches the norms (CCC 2241; EMCC 21, 30), scholars estimate the effects, legislators decide the balance, pastors accompany and do not legislate.
Step 5, STATE WHAT WOULD CHANGE YOUR MIND: write one empirical finding that would move you off your position, and note that a position that admits none has left prudential argument.

Step 6, NAME WHAT YOU WILL NOT SETTLE, and connect it to the level's earlier lessons — the bond in marriage (52), the discipline in celibacy (54), the technical determination of death (59) — each an example of a judgement the Church leaves elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A surgeon proposes an operation that will foreseeably shorten a patient's life by some months but will relieve severe pain, arguing that the pain relief outweighs the lost months. A colleague objects that the Church forbids any act that shortens life. Which analysis is correct?
questions.answer: Neither blanket claim is right: the act is analysed by its object, which is the relief of pain by a proportionate intervention, while the shortening of life is foreseen but not intended and not the means to the relief (CCC 2279; ST II-II q.64 a.7); the colleague's objection ignores intention and the surgeon's arithmetic ignores the object.
questions.distractor: The surgeon is right, because where the good effects outweigh the bad ones the act is justified, and the Church's teaching is ultimately a calculation of proportionate benefits.
questions.correction: Lesson 56's three sources decide this. The object is the proximate end chosen, which is analgesia or relief of suffering rather than death (VS 78); the intention is relief, not death; and the circumstances bear on proportionality and on culpability, not on the species of the act. That combination is what CCC 2279 permits when "death is not willed as either an end or a means, but only foreseen and tolerated as inevitable", and the underlying analysis is Aquinas's argument that one act may have two effects with only one intended (ST II-II q.64 a.7), with his own condition that excessive force in self-defence is unlawful showing that proportionality remains a requirement. The surgeon's justification fails not because the conclusion is wrong but because the reason is wrong: he has adopted a proportionalist calculation in which consequences determine the act's morality, which is precisely the thesis VS 79 rejects. The colleague's blanket objection is the mirror error, since it treats a foreseen and unintended effect as though it were intended.

questions.prompt: A politician argues that because natural-law reasoning about the family has been used to justify unjust treatment of women and of people with same-sex attraction, the natural law is a religious imposition on a plural society and should be abandoned in public argument. Which response best reflects the Church's position as presented in this unit?
questions.answer: The historical charge can be conceded without the conclusion: the tradition itself distinguishes general principles that hold without fail from the descent to detail where defects increase (ST I-II q.94 a.4; CCC 1960), and the Church holds that some moral knowledge is available to reason as such, which is what makes public argument with non-believers possible (VS 43-45).
questions.distractor: The politician is right: since the natural law has produced unjust conclusions, it is a culturally conditioned framework that cannot ground norms binding on people who do not accept its theology.
questions.correction: Lesson 57 arranged the argument in four steps — the formal first precept, the goods, the derivation of norms and their application — and showed that the criticism usually lands on the fourth step, where the tradition itself concedes that the practical reason "encounters defects" as it descends to detail (ST I-II q.94 a.4) and the Catechism acknowledges that the precepts of natural law are not perceived by everyone clearly and immediately (CCC 1960). To refute the position, an objector must attack step two by showing that a supposed good is not a perfection of the person, or step three by showing that a derivation does not follow. The Church's own defence of universal norms in Veritatis Splendor 43-53 is mounted at those levels, which is why merely citing historical misuse does not settle the question; and the objection is nonetheless worth conceding in the part where it is true, because appeals to nature have genuinely served oppressive arrangements.

questions.prompt: A manager explains that she never needed to learn any moral rules, because she has a naturally generous character and simply does what a good person does; she adds that her colleague, whose upbringing was harsh, cannot be expected to behave well. Which correction reflects this unit's account of virtue?
questions.answer: Virtue is a habit rather than a natural talent, acquired through deliberate acts and habituation and capable of growth or decay (ST I-II q.63 a.1-2; CCC 1804, 1839), so both halves of her claim are wrong: good character is something one practises rather than something one has, and it is not foreclosed to anyone by circumstances.
questions.distractor: She is right on both counts, since temperament is fixed by upbringing and the virtues are simply the outward expression of a person's natural disposition.
questions.correction: Lesson 58 set out the tradition's position: Aquinas asks whether virtue is in us by nature and answers no (ST I-II q.63 a.1), and whether any virtue is caused in us by habituation and answers yes (a.2). CCC 1804 says the moral virtues are acquired by human effort and are the fruit and seed of good acts, 1839 says they grow through education, deliberate acts and perseverance in struggle, and 1810 adds that acquired virtues are purified and elevated by grace. The second half of her claim is the more serious error, since it removes moral responsibility from the colleague on the basis of background, which the tradition does discuss — but as mitigation of culpability in particular circumstances, not as the fixed absence of a capacity for virtue. Note also what the correction does not claim: that habits are easy to form, that temperament is irrelevant, or that practical wisdom can be acquired without experience (CCC 1811).

questions.prompt: A hospital committee proposes to withdraw artificial nutrition and hydration from every patient with a diagnosis of a persistent vegetative state, in order to free beds, and asks a Catholic ethicist to endorse the policy as a legitimate withdrawal of disproportionate treatment. Which response is most accurate?
questions.answer: The policy as framed cannot be endorsed: the Holy See's 2007 responses hold that administering food and water even artificially is in principle an ordinary and proportionate means of preserving life and is therefore obligatory to the extent that and for as long as it accomplishes its proper finality, so obligatoriness must be assessed patient by patient rather than imposed categorically, and ordinary care cannot be interrupted even when death is imminent (CCC 2279).
questions.distractor: The policy is legitimate, because nutrition and hydration are always forms of medical treatment that may be withdrawn whenever the underlying condition is judged irreversible.
questions.correction: Lesson 59 required two questions to be answered in order: what is the object of the act, and what are the burdens and intention in this case? Here the policy substitutes a categorical rule for the patient-specific judgement the responses require, since they condition the obligation on whether the means "is shown to accomplish its proper finality" and on whether it causes significant physical discomfort, both of which vary between patients. A second error is embedded in the stated motive, since freeing beds is a good consequence that cannot license an act whose object is the ending of a life chosen as a means. The withdrawal of burdensome or disproportionate treatment remains legitimate in principle (CCC 2278; EV 65), and analgesia whose foreseen effect may shorten life remains legitimate under the conditions of CCC 2279, so the objection is to the categorical policy and not to the practice of limiting treatment.

questions.prompt: In a parish discussion about a proposed immigration law, one participant says the Church teaches that restrictions on immigration are intrinsically evil, and another says the Church has no authority to say anything about borders because the question is purely political. Which evaluation is correct?
questions.answer: Both statements are wrong: the Catechism obliges prosperous nations to welcome the foreigner while stating that political authorities may attach juridical conditions to immigration for the common good (CCC 2241), and the Holy See's instruction records both the right to emigrate and the power of public authorities to regulate the flow of migration (EMCC 21), so the teaching binds without prescribing one policy.
questions.distractor: The first statement is right, since the duty to welcome is taught without qualification and any restriction therefore contradicts the Church's position.
questions.correction: Both participants have taken one half of a two-sided teaching and treated it as the whole. The duty to welcome is real: CCC 2241 obliges prosperous nations "to the extent they are able", and Fratelli Tutti 121 and 124 insist that no one should be excluded by place of birth and that a country's goods must not be denied to the needy. But the same Catechism paragraph gives political authorities the power to attach conditions "for the sake of the common good for which they are responsible", and the instruction on migration states the Council's recognition of the state's right to regulate migration flows. The coherent position is therefore that the norms exclude some policies — especially any whose object instruments the suffering of persons as a means of deterrence (lesson 56; CCC 1754) — while leaving the balance of enforcement and legal pathways to prudential argument, which is why faithful Catholics defend opposing packages. The second participant's claim that the Church has no authority here is refuted by the same paragraphs the first participant quoted.

questions.prompt: Two engineers describe the same factory: one describes the machines, throughput and wage schedule; the other describes the judgements the workers make, the skills they exercise, and what their employment does to their families' lives. Which description does the Church's theology of work treat as morally decisive, and why?
questions.answer: The second: work in the subjective sense treats the acting person as the subject and beneficiary of work, and because the person is the subject, the conditions of work — including a remuneration that sustains a dignified life — are what the doctrine is about (LE 6; GS 67; CCC 2428, 2434).
questions.distractor: The first: the objective description of production and wages is what the doctrine assesses, since morality concerns the fairness of the transaction rather than the worker's experience.
