questions.correction: The two descriptions correspond to Laborem Exercens's objective and subjective senses of work, and the encyclical assigns the normative weight to the second, since the human person as a deliberative actor is what the work exists to serve: the objective elements "have only the nature of tools" (GS 67), and the Catechism's summary is that work is for man and not man for work (CCC 2428). The first description is not irrelevant — wages, hours and safety are precisely the matters the doctrine addresses — but it becomes the decisive description only if one has forgotten what the doctrine ranks above it. The practical consequence is that a wage which cannot sustain a dignified life is a moral question about an employment relation (CCC 2434), not merely an economic datum, while the choice of remedy remains prudential.

questions.prompt: A Catholic told a tribunal that her first marriage was invalid, and she now wishes to remarry in the Church. A friend objects that this is hypocrisy, since the Church says a sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved and now appears to dissolve it. How should the objection be answered?
questions.answer: A declaration of nullity is a judgement that a valid marriage never came into being for want of a required element, which is a different question from dissolving a bond, since the Church holds that she has no power to dissolve a ratified and consummated sacramental marriage (CCC 1640).
questions.distractor: The friend is right, since a declaration of nullity is the Church's way of granting a dissolution while denying that she grants dissolutions, and the moral assessment of the second marriage must therefore be negative.
questions.correction: Lesson 52 distinguished the bond, the theology that supports it, and the disciplinary application. The bond teaching is that God is the author of marriage and that the Church lacks the power to dissolve a ratified and consummated sacramental union (CCC 1640; GS 48). The tribunal's question is a different one — whether the elements required for any valid marriage were present, such as freedom, intention and form — so a nullity declaration does not perform the act the Church says she cannot perform. The friend's argument collapses two mechanisms and then draws a pastoral conclusion from an error of classification, which is the general failure this level keeps returning to: identify the kind of claim and the kind of act before evaluating it. Note the standing caveat that if the second union is celebrated without a declaration of nullity or other resolution, the pastoral situation falls under the contested application of Amoris Laetitia 300-305 rather than being settled by this answer.

questions.prompt: A retreat director describes Vatican II's teaching that the family is the domestic church and concludes that therefore every married person has a vocation to teaching the faith, so that celibate religious life is a less fruitful state than marriage. Evaluate the conclusion.
questions.answer: The premise is genuine but the conclusion does not follow: the family is called the domestic church in which parents are the first preachers of the faith (LG 11; CCC 1655-1657), and at the same time the universal call to holiness admits no state as higher, with consecrated life described as a special gift rather than a lesser profession (LG 42-43; CCC 914-916).
questions.distractor: The conclusion follows, since Vatican II taught that the family is the primary cell of the Church and that the ordinary way of holiness is marriage.
questions.correction: Two distinct teachings have been run together. That the family is the domestic church is a claim about where faith is transmitted and the priesthood of the baptized exercised (LG 11; CCC 1657). That the states of life are ordered in dignity is not taught: Lumen Gentium 39-42 grounds the call to holiness in baptism and charity rather than in state, and it describes the evangelical counsels as "a divine gift, which the Church received from its Lord" (LG 43) with consecrated life as a more intimate consecration rooted in baptism (CCC 916). Marriage and consecrated life are therefore different gifts, not ranks, and the section of this unit on the states of life made the same point about the single life, which CCC 1658 honours explicitly. The distractor also misreads Vatican II, whose teaching on marriage is that it is a genuine vocation to holiness, not that it is the ordinary route to which the counsels are subordinate.

questions.prompt: A finance director argues that the company should reduce emissions only where doing so increases profit, since the moral obligation on a business is to its shareholders and environmental concern is a personal lifestyle matter. Using this level's material, and assuming the emission reductions involve no intrinsically disordered act, which assessment is right?
questions.answer: The moral premise is wrong: creation has its own goodness and the goods of the earth are destined for all, including future generations (CCC 339, 2415, 2456; LS 159), so environmental responsibility is a duty of institutions as well as individuals, while the choice of the specific means and its timing remains a prudential judgement that the Church does not make for the firm (LS 188).
questions.distractor: The director is right, because the Church teaches that environmental questions belong to personal conscience and that a business's only moral obligation is to obey the law and serve its owners.
questions.correction: This question joins two lessons deliberately. Lesson 55 established that the ecological content of the seventh commandment binds institutions, not merely individuals: dominion is "not absolute" and "limited by concern for the quality of life of his neighbour, including generations to come" (CCC 2415), and the obligation cannot be separated from the universal destination of goods (CCC 2456). Lesson 51 supplies the parallel structure from the theology of work, where the person may not be reduced to an instrument of profit (LE 12-13; CCC 2434). What the director may legitimately claim is the prudential part: which measures, at what cost, with what effect on employment and on the poor — a question where the encyclical explicitly refuses to replace politics and where faithful Catholics disagree. The distractor therefore errs twice: it denies the taught norm and it treats as settled the prudential judgement that is genuinely open.

questions.prompt: A parish council decides to campaign for a specific housing ordinance, and a member objects that the Church has not endorsed the ordinance, so the council may not claim Catholic authority for it. How should the council proceed, on this level's account?
questions.answer: It may advocate the ordinance as a prudential application of taught principles — the common good, the priority of the poor, the duty of a just wage and the right to a home — while stating clearly that the choice of this instrument is the council's own judgement and not Church teaching (CCC 1906, 2444; GS 43, 76).
questions.distractor: The objection is decisive: because the Church has not endorsed the ordinance, a parish body may not take a public position on any specific policy question.
questions.correction: The objection identifies a real error — claiming Church authority for a prudential conclusion — and then over-corrects into a position that the documents do not support. Gaudium et Spes 43 warns against the split between faith and daily life and 76 distinguishes the tasks Christians undertake on their own responsibility as citizens from the mission of the Church, which is precisely the warrant for lay political action that does not claim to be magisterial. The correct procedure is the one lesson 55 and lesson 60 prescribe: state the taught principles with citations, state the empirical claims on which the preferred ordinance rests, state the prudential judgement as the council's own, name who holds competence, and avoid treating disagreement as infidelity. A council that does all of this speaks with integrity; a council that says "the Church teaches that we must pass this ordinance" does not.

questions.prompt: An oncology team proposes to sedate a patient into unconsciousness at his request to relieve otherwise uncontrollable suffering, knowing that the sedation will likely shorten his life, and asks whether this is euthanasia. Analysing the act, which answer is correct?
questions.answer: It is analysed by its object and intention: relieving refractory suffering by proportionate sedation is not euthanasia when death is foreseen but not willed as either the end or the means, though the practice requires that sedation be proportionate to the suffering and not a concealed way of bringing death about, which is why Samaritanus Bonus treats analgesic therapy and loss of consciousness as requiring precise conditions.
questions.distractor: It is euthanasia, because any intervention that foreseeably shortens life is an act which of itself causes death within the meaning of the Church's definition.
questions.correction: The Church's definition of euthanasia in the strict sense requires that the act or omission "of itself and by intention causes death, with the purpose of eliminating all suffering", and it locates the terms of reference "in the intention of the will and in the methods used" (EV 65; Declaration on Euthanasia II). Foreseeing a shortening of life is therefore not the same as intending death, which is the distinction CCC 2279 applies to painkillers given "even at the risk of shortening their days ... if death is not willed as either an end or a means". The double-effect structure of lesson 56 governs the analysis, including its proportionality requirement: the sedation must be measured to the suffering, not escalated to produce death. The distractor's error is to grade the act by its physical effect alone, which is the opposite error to the one it is trying to avoid.

questions.prompt: A student writes that because the natural law is grounded in what human beings naturally tend toward, and because human beings naturally tend toward sexual union and self-preservation, the natural law is simply a description of instincts and so carries no obligation. Evaluate this argument.
questions.answer: It misstates the derivation: for Aquinas the precepts of the natural law are the practical reason's grasp of goods as goods, with the first precept that good is to be done and pursued (ST I-II q.94 a.2), and the Catechism holds that the natural law expresses the original moral sense enabling reason to discern good and evil (CCC 1954), so the move is from apprehended good to obligation rather than from observed inclination to prescription.
questions.distractor: The argument is sound, and it shows that natural-law ethics is a form of biological determinism in which whatever humans tend to do becomes what they ought to do.
questions.correction: The student has skipped the step on which the entire argument turns: the practical reason's apprehension of a good as a perfection of the person, which is a rational judgement rather than a report of an impulse. This is why the tradition distinguishes what the practical reason "naturally apprehends as man's good" (ST I-II q.94 a.2) from what people happen to desire, and why Veritatis Splendor 78-80 insists that the object of a moral act is the proximate end of a deliberate decision rather than a physical process. The student's argument is worth engaging rather than dismissing, because the strongest objection to natural-law ethics is precisely the derivation problem: the is/ought gap must be bridged, and the traditional school bridges it by appeal to goods and inclinations while the newer school appeals to self-evident practical truths. What cannot be done is to describe the position as biological determinism, which misrepresents both schools.

questions.prompt: A department head who has always acted fairly is suddenly placed under severe pressure and behaves worse than a colleague with a documented history of small dishonesties who is placed under comparable pressure. Does this falsify the Catholic account of virtue?
questions.answer: No: the account claims that habits shape a person's dispositions and practical judgement and that virtue grows through repeated acts and grace, not that character produces uniform behaviour under pressure, which is the difference between the tradition's normative account and the predictive claim the situationist critique attacks.
questions.distractor: Yes, since the case shows that behaviour is determined by situation rather than character, and the tradition's claim that virtue shapes conduct is therefore refuted.
questions.correction: The situationist critique attributed to Doris, Harman and others does show that cross-situational behavioural consistency is weaker than trait psychology once assumed, and this lesson does not pretend otherwise. But the critique addresses a predictive version of the claim. The tradition's claims are different in kind: that virtue is a habit acquired by deliberate acts (ST I-II q.63 a.1-2; CCC 1804, 1839); that it disposes the appetites so that practical reason can judge well about particulars (CCC 1806; ST II-II q.47 a.3); and that the moral life is sustained by grace, since maintaining moral balance is not easy for a person wounded by sin (CCC 1811). A single failure under severe pressure is compatible with all three, and indeed the tradition expects lapses and provides for repentance; a pattern of collapse, by contrast, would be evidence that the habit was never formed. Notice also that the case as stated compares two people rather than measuring the same person over time, which is the wrong experimental design for a claim about habituation.

questions.prompt: A Catholic legislator votes for a bill that expands research using cell lines derived from embryos destroyed years ago, arguing that the bill also funds treatments for a disease that kills thousands every year. The bill contains no provision for alternative cell lines or for the registration of objection. Which evaluation follows from this level's material?
questions.answer: The objection duty matters: Dignitas Personae 34 permits the use of illicit-origin biological material only with differentiated responsibility and "grave reasons", and it insists that those who use it have the duty to make their disagreement known and to press for alternatives, so a bill that replaces that duty with permanent acceptance does not meet the standard the document sets.
questions.distractor: The bill is permissible without qualification, since once the destruction has occurred the material is simply available, and funding treatments that save lives is plainly a proportionate good.
questions.correction: Dignitas Personae 34 is unusual because it grants a permission and then attaches conditions that are part of the permission rather than optional refinements: the material comes from an act against human life, the connection may be mediate or immediate, cooperation must be assessed, and those who benefit have "the duty to make known their disagreement and to ask that their healthcare system make other types of vaccines available". The distractor both overstates the permission and omits the conditions, which is why it fails. Note the second half of the analysis, which keeps it from becoming formalism: the good the legislator pursues is real, and the document itself speaks of grave reasons that can make use proportionate, so the objection is not to compromise as such but to institutionalising the compromise with no register of dissent and no pressure toward alternatives. Behind the case sits the level's standing distinction between a norm that binds and an application that must be argued.

questions.prompt: A Catholic magazine asks a writer to defend the claim that the magisterium's teaching on the family has not changed while the pastoral practice of different dioceses plainly has. How should the writer frame the piece?
questions.answer: By distinguishing the layers: the definition and the bond (CCC 1601, 1640) are taught and unchanged; the theology of marriage (FC 13) is argued; and the pastoral discipline implementing Amoris Laetitia 300-305 is authoritative but contested in its application and implemented differently, so practice can vary without the doctrine having moved.
questions.distractor: By arguing that the differences in practice prove that the doctrine has in fact changed, since pastoral practice is the only reliable evidence of what a Church teaches.
questions.correction: The distractor adopts the principle that practice measures doctrine, which would make any administrative variation a doctrinal revolution. The more accurate frame is the one taught in lesson 52 and used throughout this level: identify the kind of claim first. The definition and the indissolubility of a ratified and consummated sacramental marriage are taught as divine disposition (CCC 1601, 1640), the theology that grounds them is argued (FC 13), and the pastoral application following Amoris Laetitia is where bishops have implemented differing norms and where the argument continues. That frame allows the writer to say two true things at once: that a Catholic may not treat the bond teaching as optional, and that a critic is entitled to argue that a particular application is inconsistent with the doctrine — an argument that is legitimate precisely because it is about the application. Compare lesson 54, where the celibacy discipline likewise persists unchanged while nothing forbids arguing about it.

questions.prompt: A community group asks a parish to endorse a ballot measure on assisted suicide that criminalises assisting suicide while, in a separate clause, also restricts pain-treatment funding. Which response follows from the analysis in this unit?
questions.answer: The parish may support the provision that upholds the prohibition on direct killing and must oppose or condition its support on the clause that withholds relief of suffering, because the Church holds both that direct euthanasia and assisted suicide are excluded (CCC 2277; EV 65) and that ordinary care and pain relief, including analgesia with foreseen risk, are owed to the dying (CCC 2279; Samaritanus Bonus on palliative care).
questions.distractor: The parish should endorse the measure as it stands, because opposing assisted suicide is the only morally relevant feature and the funding clause is a political detail outside the parish's competence.
questions.correction: The measure sets two morally loaded provisions against each other, which is the situation that requires the analysis of acts rather than a single-issue reflex. On the first clause the Church's prohibition is defined teaching and not a matter for prudential weighing: direct euthanasia is "an act or omission which, of itself or by intention, causes death, with the purpose of eliminating all suffering" and is morally unacceptable (CCC 2277; EV 65). On the second clause the teaching is equally clear that the dying are owed ordinary care that cannot be interrupted even when death is imminent, and that palliative care is a form of charity (CCC 2279), which is why the parish cannot treat the funding restriction as an indifferent detail. The distractor reduces a two-part act to one feature; the opposite error, refusing to engage the measure at all because it is mixed, abdicates the lay competence that Gaudium et Spes 43 and 76 assign to citizens.

questions.prompt: A student concludes this level by saying that the Church's teaching is useless for real decisions because it always ends in "it depends" and never tells anyone what to do. Using at least three lessons, evaluate the claim.
questions.answer: The claim conflates the absence of one answer with the absence of constraints: the Church defines acts that may never be chosen — direct abortion, deliberate destruction of embryos, direct euthanasia, deliberate killing of the innocent (CCC 2271, 2277; DP 21-22; EV 57) — and derives duties of welcome, just wages, indissolubility of a ratified and consummated sacramental marriage, and respect for one's own body and property, while leaving the choice of means, the measurement of burdens and the design of policy to prudence exercised by competent people in formed conscience.
questions.distractor: The claim is right as stated, since a teaching that leaves the choice of means to individuals has no normative content and can be made to support any position.
questions.correction: The claim mistakes a division of labour for an absence of content, and the level supplies three counterexamples at increasing distance from individual cases. First, the moral method of lesson 56 establishes that some acts are excluded by their object, quite apart from consequences: the manager who orders a falsified safety report, the physician who intends a patient's death, the researcher who destroys embryos as a research step. Second, lesson 59 shows the definiteness of the prohibitions and their scope at both ends of life. Third, lessons 55 and 60 show the same structure in social questions: real norms — the goodness of creation and its destination for all; the duty of prosperous nations to welcome while authorities may set juridical conditions for the common good (CCC 2241) — and then a genuinely prudential remainder. What the Church does not do is supply a decision procedure that could be run without prudence, experience, counsel and grace, and the fact that the difficult part falls on the agent is not a defect in a teaching that exists to form agents. The distractor's error is the mirror of a slogan: it treats the absence of a single answer as the absence of any answer.
